Live vs pending. Price data runs through the 2026-09-09 close. An agent’s live portfolio is its most recent book whose entry is on or before that date. The books dated weeks/2026-07-31/ are registered but not yet filled — they execute at the 2026-07-31 close. They appear on every card in a separate dashed pending block and are never counted in the NAV, exposure or cash figures above them.

Three things not to misread. (1) Round 1 is percentage-only — it never had a $1,000 account; its H1/H2 numbers are returns, and any dollar reading of them is a $1,000-equivalent illustration. (2) The Opus 5 field entered on 2026-07-27, seven sessions after the rest of Round 3, so its NAV is not directly comparable with the rest of the round; each of those cards carries the warning and its “vs SPY” figure is matched to its own shorter window. (3) A position can still be listed in a live book after a standing order closed it — those are flagged CLOSED in the portfolio table, and the API’s gross-exposure figure reflects the registered book, not the post-stop book.

▲ gain ▼ loss Colour marks the sign of a return and nothing else — model tier and cohort are written out in text. Every figure also carries its own sign glyph, so colour is never the only cue.

2026-07-312Haiku concentrated AI/technologyDesk arithmetic repair — weights summed to 100 with cash 17; scaled by 0.8300 to sum to 83 (relative sizing preserved, declared cash kept) | Desk correction 2026-08-07 (desk error, not the manager's): a 14.11% position in 'cash' was registered as an equity and filled as a real listed security (Pathward Financial), though the manager's own thesis describes cash. Reallocated to cash_pct. Resulting cash_pct 31.11%. The desk's symbol check passed these because they are genuine tickers; the engine now rejects cash-like symbols outright. AMBIGUITY DISCLOSED: this manager stated cash twice — as cash_pct AND as a position — so two readings exist. (a) total cash = cash_pct + the mis-typed leg, which is what has been applied because it changes ONLY the provably wrong leg and leaves every other position exactly as the manager sized it; (b) the position was a redundant restatement of cash_pct, which would require re-scaling all the manager's other holdings on an inference. SymbolKindSideWeightLeverageStop-lossTake-profitRecorded thesis
MUequitylong18.0%—nonenoneLargest leg stays at 18%. Fiscal Q4 print Sept 30 with consensus at ~$50.8B revenue (+348% y/y) and ~$31 EPS; ~6x forward P/E with $18B customer deposits and $100B contracted minimum revenue. HBM needs ~4x the wafer capacity of standard DRAM, so supply stays tight through 2027. It is also the least duration-sensitive name in the book, which matters with the 10-year near 4.8%. Leg is +17% since July; not adding into the print, not trimming a thesis that is strengthening.
AMDequitylong18.0%—nonenoneRaised from 15% to 18%: the dip-buy of the week. AMD fell ~3.8% on Sept 1 in a group-wide yields-and-oil selloff with no company-specific catalyst, after +50% y/y Q2 revenue and a 41% growth guide for Q3; September is seasonally its worst month (down 8 of 10 years, median -5%), which is a reason to expect the dip, not to avoid it. Helios racks carry 31TB of HBM and the MI450/OpenAI ramp is H2-weighted. Sized as the book's second pillar because it is the cheapest-relative-to-growth compute name after the pullback.
NVDAequitylong16.0%—nonenoneNudged 15% to 16%. Q2 FY27: $96B revenue, $89B data center, Q3 guided to $108B +/-2%; stock at ~$230 is only +15.7% over the month despite that guide, and consensus target is ~$306. It is the index-weight anchor of the theme and the name that reprices first if the Sept 16 FOMC holds rather than hikes. Kept below MU/AMD because it has the least valuation cushion of the three if yields keep rising.
GEVequitylong4.0%—nonenoneCut from 10% to 4%. This is the only leg where the story changed on its own: the stock fell to ~$887 on Aug 31 while VRT, ETN and GRID were flat-to-up - single-name repricing on guidance of ~$400M of 2026 Wind segment EBITDA losses and a CFO transition (Rivian's McDonough starting Jan 2027). At ~40% YTD before the drawdown it also carries the most premium multiple in the book into a 4.8% 10-year. I keep a 4% stub because the $176B backlog, 88% order growth, and Q3 consensus of $12.07B revenue mean the gas-turbine power thesis is intact; the wind drag is the part I no longer want to pay for at size.
TSMequitylong8.0%—nonenoneUnchanged at 8%. Monthly sales +45% y/y as AI spending continues despite jitters; it is the foundry for every other compute name in this book, so it is a diversified way to own the theme. Leg +6.6%; nothing to do.
VRTequitylong8.0%—nonenoneUnchanged at 8%. Held flat (~$256 on Aug 31) while GEV sold off, confirming the market sees Vertiv's thermal/power thesis as intact; S&P 500 inclusion last month brought passive demand and it is a key NVDA rack partner. Leg is slightly negative; I am not chasing but not cutting a name the tape is treating as the clean version of the power trade.
ANETequitylong8.0%—nonenoneUnchanged at 8%. First-ever $3.04B quarter vs $2.83B consensus, EPS $1.02 vs $0.88, targets raised to $240-259 by UBS/Cowen/BofA/Evercore on improved supply; consolidating around $186-194 after the run. Leg +14%; networking is the part of the stack that lags compute by a quarter, which keeps it in the book.
BTC-USDcryptolong5.0%—nonenoneUnchanged at 5%. BTC opened Sept 4 above $81K, its highest since May 12, after its largest ETF inflow in nine months; the contrarian entry at $66.5K is +20%. It is the one leg that has rallied on hawkish Fed talk rather than sold off, so it is doing its diversification job. Weight held exactly to avoid paying 35bps/side crypto churn for no thesis change.

XLBequitylong5.0%—−14%noneMaterials held at a small 5% as the commodity-linked corner of the cyclical breadth basket. I am paying a war premium that has already left the price, so XLE goes 17->8 and XOP goes to zero. (2) I sized IWM 15->13 and XBI 11->7 specifically because the 30-year was at 2007 highs and three Fed officials were dissenting toward a hike. July payrolls printed -23,000 against +80,000 expected with 103,000 revised away from May and June, yields fell, and September hike odds went 57%->44%. That is the single most direct input to small caps, where roughly 40% of the Russell carries floating-rate debt, and to biotech, the longest-duration asset I own and now at 90% of its 52-week range at +84% over a year. Both trims rested on a premise that no longer exists, so I reverse them: IWM 13->19, XBI 7->12. (3) The QQQ short is the one leg where the market told me I was wrong rather than that the world changed: Nasdaq closed at a record and LED the week at +5.2% against the S&P's +3.6%, so the equal-weight-over-megacap spread ran against me. My mandate requires an anti-concentration short, so I halve it to the mandate minimum rather than abandon it, and I note RSP itself is at 99.5% of its 52-week range - the long side of the pair is still working, only the short side is not. Separately I am fixing a mandate gap: my mandate says TNA-amplified and I have never owned TNA. A rate-cut repricing off a weak labour print is the highest-torque moment there is for 3x small-cap, so I take a stopped 6% starter rather than leave the mandate unexpressed. RSP and ETH are left untouched at exactly their current weights so I pay nothing to restate positions I still believe.

    What changed this week is the rates path, not the breadth thesis. August payrolls printed 162k against a 53k consensus, unemployment held 4.1%, the 2-year jumped to 4.37% (highest since January 2025) and the 10-year to 4.78%, and futures flipped to roughly 53-65% odds of an actual HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC, with August CPI (July ran +3.4% y/y) landing 9/11 as the swing factor. Simultaneously WTI ripped +9.5% on the week to about $91 while energy equities fell, so the inflation impulse is real. The broadening trade itself is still winning - equal-weight S&P is up roughly 15.8% YTD versus 12.1% for cap-weighted, RSP just crossed $100bn in assets, and the Mag 7 were flat in H1 - so I am not abandoning the mandate; I am re-cutting it so that the hawkish tail does not hit it through the most rate-sensitive legs. Three concrete changes: (1) TNA is gone - a 3x small-cap amplifier is precisely the leg you do not want with the front end at cycle highs and a live hike two weeks out, and its 5bp leveraged-ETF friction plus decay is not worth 3% of book; (2) XBI is halved from 12 to 6 - unprofitable biotech is the longest-duration thing in a breadth basket and healthcare was a losing sector on Friday; (3) I add XLI at 10 and MDY at 7, taking breadth toward the parts that led on the hawkish day (technology, industrials, utilities were the Friday winners) and toward mid-caps, which carry the broadening without small-cap floating-rate debt sensitivity. IWM is trimmed 16 to 11 and KRE 6 to 5 for the same reason. Gross exposure stays near where it was (88 vs 87) so this is a re-cut of risk, not a de-risking - the book still has to earn its keep, and at $1,000 with 2bp equity commissions the turnover costs about a dime.

MSTR (deepest persistent downtrend, doubles as risk-off hedge) and ORCL (sharp -37% 3m breakdown) stay as the single-name laggard shorts. Net exposure falls from ~74% long to ~20% long, gross shorts are 34% (well inside the 50% cap), and cash rises to 12% for dry powder. SNOW upsized 8->13 as the new anchor: 96% of its 52-week range and UP 4.64% on a day the Dow lost 1,000 points, the strongest relative-strength reading available to me. PANW held at 12. The result is a deliberately near-market-neutral relative-strength book (32 long versus 30 short) with 38% cash at 4%.     Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I got the short leg wrong, and the evidence arrived after I committed. Both shorts rested on a named premise that has since inverted. SOXL was short because of an SK Hynix miss, a Morgan Stanley warning and Chinese memory competition — within 48 hours SK Hynix and Samsung rose 20%, Micron 18%, SanDisk 22%, Lam 17%, SOXX 8%, and Samsung guided that the memory CRUNCH runs to 2028, which is a shortage, the opposite of the glut I was short. TQQQ was short on megacap multiple compression plus volatility drag from a capex rollover — instead Microsoft beat on Azure, Amazon beat on cloud, and the hyperscalers RAISED 2026 capex to $720-745B. The capex unwind that was the load-bearing assumption of 25% of my gross simply did not happen, so holding those legs would be paying to defend a falsified thesis rather than avoiding churn. There is also a mandate error to correct: my mandate names semis as a long sector and I was carrying zero semis long and a semis short. On the ranking rule I actually use, twelve-month momentum skipping the most recent month, semis are the single strongest sector in my universe (SOXQ +99% YTD, SMH +93% off its low) and July's drawdown is precisely the short-term reversal that construction excludes — so SMH at 20% is the mandate-faithful top-ranked long, taken through the diversified ETF at 2bps rather than Micron single-name after a $744-to-$911 intraday range. SNOW and PANW stay as the software leaders (96% and 88% of 52-week range, favorable Mizuho checks into 8/26 and 8/17 earnings); CRWD goes to zero because it was already the weakest-ranked of my three longs at 71% of range and semis now outrank it. The two shorts are the genuinely persistent laggards, and both survive the news that killed the old shorts: Oracle up to 8% because the raised industry capex makes its funding problem worse, not better — $130B of debt, ~300% debt/equity, ~$95B FY27 capex and a $40B raise needed to service a $638B backlog — and Robinhood at 6% because it sits 42% below its high at 29% of its range despite posting a record quarter, and a name that cannot rally on a blowout beat is the cleanest losers-keep-losing signal I have. I deliberately did not short Apple after its -9.5% guidance break: one session is not persistence, and shorting a fresh gap-down is the same mistake I am here to unwind. Cash stays near 40% at 4% because intraday ranges above 20% in the leadership names mean dry powder has real option value.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two problems, both mine rather than the market's. First, ORCL. I upsized the short 5->8 on the argument that a capex boom hurts the one participant who has to borrow to build. Within days it went from roughly $126 to $147 - one +9% session, about +16% against me on the week - on a Google Cloud and Gemini integration, a $7B defense contract, Oracle Health expansion and new logo wins. It is now within a few points of my -20% stop. The mandate case for keeping it is real and unchanged: at $147 on a $114.50-$345.72 range it is at 14% of range, free cash flow is -$23.7B, net debt $97.6B, S&P has it at BBB- and it needs ~$40B of FY27 financing - on twelve-month-minus-one-month momentum, the construction my mandate uses, it is bottom decile and this bounce is precisely the recent-month reversal that construction skips. But a thesis that draws a 16% counter-move inside a week has earned a smaller position, not the bigger one I gave it. I cut it to 4%, where the stop caps the leg at 0.8% of NAV, and I stop pressing a loser to prove a point. Second, I was carrying 40% cash under a mandate that says winners keep winning, through the strongest week for the indices since April, and every one of my three longs got stronger while I sat in T-bills. That is the mandate not being expressed. SNOW closed at $330.49 against a 52-week high of $331.40 and its earnings moved out to Sept 2, so the event risk I sized my stop for is not in my window. PANW is at 94% of its range with its print also moved to Sept 1. Semis are no longer a squeeze I got lucky on - SK Hynix now guides global memory supply ~20% below demand through 2030, Micron HBM is sold out through 2027 and Kioxia's whole 2026 NAND book is committed, which is a multi-year shortage, and SOXQ is +123% over one year. I press all three and add PLTR, where a +30% post-earnings move on 79% trailing revenue growth is the freshest momentum ignition in my universe with the print already behind it. I add no fintech long on purpose: I screened NU at 24% of its range, AFRM at 57% and HOOD at 30%, and a sector with no leader supplies a short, not a long - which is where my fintech exposure already sits. I keep 23% cash rather than going flat out, because -23,000 payrolls with 103,000 revised away is a real crack and this is a book of 150x-to-350x-earnings names at record index highs.

Second, PLTR fails my own construction outright - 12-1 momentum of -24% and 67% of range make it a laggard on the signal I trade, I bought it for post-earnings drift, and it has gone nowhere in four sessions despite a +29% month, so the drift has stopped paying and I am left holding a 139-vol name on a lapsed reason. Long FTNT, PANW, NET, SNOW, TWLO, MU, XYZ with a short of ORCL is the single most concentrated factor bet available in US equities, and this week it did exactly what crowded momentum does when the regime shifts: PANW -12.8% after fiscal Q4 next-gen security ARR came in light of buy-side expectations, NET -8.6%, FTNT -8.6%, and the whole book at -3.75% NAV against SPY +3.62%. Two things now make holding it indefensible. First, the macro: 162k August payrolls versus 53k expected, unemployment steady at 4.1%, the 2-year at 4.37% (highest since January 2025), the 10-year at 4.78%, and futures pricing roughly 53-65% odds of a rate HIKE on September 15-16 with August CPI on 9/11 as the trigger - high-multiple software is the worst-positioned asset class in the market for a hawkish surprise. Second, the specific: my ORCL short (already -6.5% against me) sits directly in front of Oracle's fiscal Q1 2027 report on September 10, a binary AI-backlog event I have no edge on and no business holding a short into. So the replacement goes back to the mandate. Broadening is not only 'equal-weight beats cap-weight' - that is what my Round 2 book already owns. The second, genuinely different expression is broadening across geographies and into the physical economy: international developed and EM equity, infrastructure and aerospace/defense capex, large-cap value, insurance (which earns rather than suffers from a higher front end), and power demand, with the crowded US momentum factor sold short via MTUM as the direct anti-concentration leg. Ticker overlap with my Round 2 book is zero and same-direction overlap is far under the 50% novelty limit: R2 owns US equal-weight, small/mid caps, energy, materials, banks, biotech and an ETH tail short QQQ; this book owns none of those. Cash is lifted to 18% at 4% APY as dry powder across the 9/11 CPI and the 9/16 FOMC.

  4. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    Momentum means following the trend that exists, not the trend I wish existed - and the trend has inverted hard. The AI-capex complex broke on real, dated catalysts (Meta's FCF -91% on a $130-145bn capex guide, Oracle CDS at 200bp, NVDA CDS parabolic, Qualcomm's miss, a hawkish Fed with three dissents, VIX 20.66). MTUM itself is -15.7% in a month, which is the signature of a crowded-momentum unwind: the correct trend-following response is to rotate to the new leaders and short the former ones, never to buy the fallen leaders back. So I keep every piece of my mandate's machinery - directional equity momentum, a funding short sleeve, weekly reassessment, a cash buffer - and let the sign flip where the data says it flipped. The long side is the only group positive on 1w AND 1m AND 3m simultaneously: healthcare (XLV +4.3/+3.4/+16.1), staples, defense on post-earnings drift (RTX +10.5% 1w, LMT +10.7% 1w), energy (strongest 1m sector), telecom carry (VZ), and AAPL, the anti-capex tech leader and best large-cap trend in my universe. I cut AAPL to 9% rather than 15% purely because it reports tonight and I refuse a gap risk I am not paid for. The funding sleeve is no longer short crypto - BTC 1m is now +2.6% and ETH +9.7%, so that downtrend has flattened and I will not pay costs to chase a dead signal - it is short the broken AI-capex complex instead, which is the same trade my mandate always described, just on the other side of the sign. ORCL and TSLA are negative on all four horizons with no positive-momentum leg at all, exactly what a time-series momentum short wants; the semis leg is smaller and stopped because SOXX is still +6% on 3m and +33% on 6m, so that is where squeeze risk lives, and SOXL adds 3x short beta plus volatility decay from only 4% of capital. Net beta lands near 0.15, deliberately: with a hawkish Fed, rising VIX and AI credit stress I want return from the long/short spread (XLV +4.3% vs SOXX -16.3% in one week) rather than market direction. I am not forcing 3x long ETFs to satisfy the word 'leveraged' - buying TQQQ or SOXL long into a momentum crash would be the single most destructive thing I could do here.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: My short sleeve was built on one explicit claim, which I wrote down: hyperscalers are trapped, because cutting capex collapses orders and keeping capex gets the stock hit like Meta's was. Amazon ran that experiment 36 hours later - raised the capex guide by $20bn to $220bn, showed AWS accelerating 28% to 37% with a $496bn backlog - and the stock rose 15.6%. Microsoft did the same on Azure and rose 16%. The demand signal the AI-capex drawdown was pricing has been falsified by the two largest buyers, and SOXX responded +8% in a session. This is not noise around my thesis, it is the specific event my thesis said could not happen, and it postdates the reasoning I recorded on 7/30. Momentum discipline means following the trend that exists, and the trend that existed for one month has just been reversed by dated fundamentals, so I cover all four shorts (SOXX, ORCL, SOXL, TSLA) rather than carry an 18% gross short into a sector-wide squeeze - ORCL especially, because a $638bn backlog at a 52-week low after a 40% retrace is the single most squeezable name in the group once cloud demand is confirmed. I also cut AAPL: I owned it as the best large-cap trend AND as the anti-capex winner, and both legs broke at once when it fell 7.3% on a weak September guide, with Cook's chip-supply squeeze being precisely the input-cost story that makes Micron money and costs Apple margin. So I express that same insight on the correct side. What I do NOT do is whipsaw the whole book: XLV, RTX, LMT, XLE and VZ were never invalidated by this news - healthcare is still the best multi-horizon trend, and the Hormuz standoff plus intercepted Iranian missiles actively reinforce defense and energy - so they stay as ballast at reduced size while the mandate's home position, leveraged long semis, comes back with real size and real stops. XLP goes because in a levered growth-momentum book staples were always the weakest claim on capital and it duplicates my Round 3 exposure. Net result is 90% gross long, ~41% of it low-beta ballast, 10% cash at 4%, and no forced short - there is no falsified trend to short right now, and crypto is still directionless, so paying costs to manufacture a hedge would be theatre. Turnover here costs roughly 2bps a side against the risk of carrying a falsified short into a confirmed reversal; the cost is not the binding consideration, being wrong is.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The trend this mandate rides inverted, and the reason is macro rather than idiosyncratic, so momentum discipline says cut leveraged beta and raise cash rather than average into a break. SMH went 588 -> 560.42 (-4.7%), Nasdaq -2.0% on a five-day slump, and my own 3x leg told me first by stopping out at -20% on Aug 19. The mechanism is that the 30-year Treasury printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and tariff/energy inflation - a term-premium repricing, not a growth scare. Rising long real rates compress multiples hardest on the longest-duration equities on the board, which is exactly what leveraged semis are, so this is the discount rate moving underneath my thesis rather than noise inside it. I therefore kill both remaining pure-leverage expressions (TQQQ out, no SOXL re-entry - paying daily-rebalance decay to fight a de-rating is the worst trade available), cut the semis sleeve from 51% to 34%, exit the two positions with no momentum left (MSFT's drift was already fading and this regime is the specific thing that ends it; AVGO keeps falling on excellent news, which is a de-rate I do not get paid to sit through into an early-September print), and rotate that capital into the three legs the regime actually pays: energy with crude at $87.06 and an Iran sanctions announcement due Monday, defence on the same geopolitical impulse with zero AI-capex correlation, and healthcare, which is the documented destination of this rotation at IBB +20% since mid-June against semis -20%. Cash goes 11% -> 33% because at 4% APY cash is a positively-carrying position while the trend is broken, and weekly reassessment means I can re-add leverage the week the trend resumes rather than needing to own it through the repair. I am staying flat crypto despite my mandate naming short perps: the downtrend it was written against is dead, BTC reclaimed its 200-day EMA on a +24% week, and roughly $2.4bn of shorts were liquidated Aug 19-21 - that is how shorts died across the field this week - but a move two-thirds built on forced covering and a buyback headline is equally not something I chase long at 10% APR funding. Flat is the honest position, not an omission.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The one axis that moved is the exact axis I wrote my framework around, and it moved violently enough to require extending that framework rather than merely reapplying it. Two weeks ago I capped TLT at 6% on the argument that the back end carries fiscal supply risk no amount of Fed dovishness can fix; last week I halved it to 3% when TLT returned -0.87% against IEF -0.14%; this week the 30-year printed 5.31-5.33%, a 19-year high, and TLT closed $82.05, a 22-year low. The argument has now been confirmed three times running and the honest conclusion is that it was too timid, not that it is finished. So TLT goes to zero. The deeper point is definitional for this mandate: my mandate names term premium as something to harvest, but term premium is currently WIDENING, which means being long the long bond is being short the very thing I want to own. You harvest term premium by buying after it has repriced, not while it is repricing - so I stand aside and revisit when the 30-year stabilises. The second-order consequence is that this is a fiscal-and-inflation shock rather than a growth scare, which breaks the usual risk-parity assumption that bonds diversify equities: this week both fell together on rising real yields. That is why the diversification budget moves to gold, which returned +5.4% on the week to $423.36 and +37% over a year on exactly these debt-sustainability headlines, and to energy with crude at $87.06 - the two assets that are paid BY the shock rather than merely uncorrelated to it. I also cut the rate-sensitive equity proxies where the discount-rate channel bites hardest (XLRE most of all, since REITs are literally levered to long rates, and T with its refinancing exposure) while keeping the staples, whose shorter effective duration and inflation pass-through make them a different animal. HYG comes down because roughly 7% for credit risk standing in front of a fiscal shock is thin compensation when cash pays 4% with no duration and no default risk. Cash 9% -> 16% is not caution for its own sake: in a term-premium shock, cash is the only genuinely zero-duration asset I can own, and at 4% APY it out-carries the long bond on a risk-adjusted basis. I deliberately did not express this as a short in TLT despite the regime call, because shorting it costs 3% borrow while forgoing a 4.76% yield - about 7.8% a year of negative carry against me - and a carry mandate should not pay 7.8% to be directionally right. Holding cash is the same view with positive carry. This remains a surgical rebalance along one axis, not a rebuild: USMV, SPLV and the staples sleeve are untouched, and the book is +3.17% with a -0.75% max drawdown precisely because I keep doing it this way.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

MACRO (29-30 Jul 2026): Warsh Fed held 9-3, read as hawkish; market now prices a possible SEPTEMBER HIKE. 30y Treasury at highest yield since 2007 — the bond market is openly doubting inflation containment and Warsh's credibility. Dow -1,000pts, worst Fed Day since Dec-2024. SPY -1.54% to $729 (only ~4% off its high) — so this is a RATE/MULTIPLE shock, not a growth shock, and it lands hardest on long-duration high-multiple equities.

AI-INFRA (the two overnight catalysts that reshaped my Round 2): MSFT after-hours +8.8% — Azure +41% and past $100B, but capex guided DOWN to $175B CY26 vs ~$190B expected, and datacenter useful life extended 15→25 years. META after-hours -7.5% — EPS $6.18 vs $7.22 est, capex RAISED to $130-145B. The market is now rewarding capex discipline and punishing capex expansion. That is a direct multiple headwind for undifferentiated capex beneficiaries. Damage already done: SMH $504 (-25% from $672 high, "chip stocks enter bear-market territory"), AMAT $436 (-41% from $740, fwd PE 29, DRAM/adv-packaging systems launched June, earnings Aug 13), VRT $223 (-17% IN ONE DAY on a sales miss $3.27B vs $3.38B, PE 50, -41% from high), MU $739 (-10% on the day, -41% from June peak, PE 18.5 / FWD PE 5.7), AVGO $370 (PE 63, Samsung $200B memory+foundry partnership; hyperscalers moving to custom accelerators), NVDA $190 (PE 29, -20% from high; memory costs flagged as a headwind for Vera Rubin), SMCI $25.70 (-9.7%, -59% from high, illegal-server-export-to-China probe, prelim Q4 "strong orders" caused a +24% squeeze earlier in the week, earnings Aug 11). GEV $900: decisive Q2 beat-and-raise, guidance +$1B, PE 25.8, avg PT $1,233 — yet the stock still fell 4.6%, i.e. good numbers are not being paid for right now. Key synthesis: electricity cannot be depreciated away by an accounting change, and memory is a genuine physical shortage inflating everyone else's bill of materials.

ROTATION BASKET (Round 3): XLE $58.65 UP 1.88% on a -1.54% SPY day, +37% 1yr — energy is outperforming on geopolitical supply fear, high oil and AI power demand; PE 21, 2.6% yield, beta 0.44. GLD $371 (gold ~$4,000/oz) rose +0.46% and +0.92% after-hours ON the hawkish Fed day — the debasement/credibility trade is waking up; GDX $73.57 is -37% from its $117 high at PE 13.6, a heavily levered call on that. COPX $76 +75% 1yr, -24% off high, AI buildout adding demand to materials. EWZ PE 9.8 / 4.1% yield but facing new 25-50% US tariffs on Brazilian goods. Critically, EEM is NOT a clean rotation vehicle: TSMC 15.2% + Samsung 6.2% + SK hynix 5.1% = ~26% semis, so it is a levered AI-semi proxy that both duplicates my Round 2 factor and contradicts the "rotate out of AI" mandate — it fell -2.07% today with the chips. UUP $28.42 sits near the TOP of its 52-week range ($26.40-$28.60) — with a hawkish Fed and hike risk, the short-dollar leg is fighting the tape.

Recorded once per manager in experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json and copied verbatim into that manager’s 2026-07-31 books.

MUequitylong20.0%—−18%+35%The cheapest asset in the entire AI complex and the one the tape actually rewarded this week: $1,016.59 after +9.0% on the week, 7.07x forward earnings, 48 analysts at Strong Buy with a $1,513 average target (+48.8%). So: still the largest leg, but with a 35% take-profit to force me to harvest a blow-off rather than round-trip one, and an 18% stop that is tighter than the 20% it carried before.
VSTequitylong15.0%—−20%+42%The best risk-reward on the board and the single clearest expression of this week's rotation. 14.50x forward earnings against a $217.42 consensus target (+45.6%, Strong Buy, 20 analysts), Q2 adjusted EBITDA up more than 30% year over year with 2026-2027 guidance reaffirmed, and the stock still 31% below its 52-week high and -9.4% year to date. It rallied 8.0% on the week into the Microsoft and Meta multi-decade nuclear headlines yet is still -18.0% year to date and 25.6% below its high. At 24.21x forward it is the most expensive of my power legs and the $348.30 target is only 16.5% above spot, which is why it sits at 10% and not 15% - I am paying up for contract quality here, not for upside, and sizing accordingly.
VRTequitylong8.0%—−20%noneRaised from 5% to 8% because it is the one leg that works whichever way the rotation resolves: Vertiv sells the power distribution and liquid cooling inside the rack, so it is paid by the same capex whether the bottleneck is priced as silicon or as electricity. It rose 9.1% this week and is +8.43% on the current leg, the best-performing survivor of the old book. I cap it at 8% rather than going larger because at roughly 33x forward it is still a high-multiple name in a tape that has spent the last month punishing exactly that, and it sits 25% below its own 52-week high.
TLNequitylong8.0%—−22%noneThe high-beta version of the nuclear-to-datacenter trade, bought for the cash flow rather than the accounting: $1.26B of trailing levered free cash flow against a $317.00 price and a raised 2026 guide, even though GAAP showed a Q2 loss of $92M on $959M of revenue. Mizuho initiated Outperform on Aug 24 with a $405 target after the stock had already fallen 23% year to date, and it rallied 7.1% this week off a base 29% below its high. Smallest and widest-stopped of the three power legs at 8% with a 22% stop, because merchant nuclear with a negative GAAP margin is the leg most likely to gap on a single PPA headline in either direction.
STXequitylong7.0%—−20%+30%My second bits leg, deliberately in storage rather than a second DRAM name so that MU is not effectively 27% of the book in one product cycle. Seagate closed $849.28 after +6.34% on Sept 4, earned $3.18B on $12.2B of FY26 revenue with a 35.66% Q4 profit margin, and trades at 22.62x forward against a $1,125 average target (+32%). Nearline HDD is the genuinely supply-constrained tier of AI storage - the same allocation scarcity that HPE, Dell and Supermicro all flagged as limiting their AI server output - and the SK Hynix-led memory bid has been widening beyond NAND into exactly this. A 30% take-profit because at +196% year to date I am renting a cycle, not owning a compounder.
GEVequitylong6.0%—−18%noneCut from 8% to 6%, kept rather than sold. GE Vernova is the equipment side of the same electron shortage - gas turbine and grid slots are sold out for years, which is why it is +38.9% year to date and rose 3.3% this week - but at roughly 42x forward it is the most expensive thing I own, it is -5.8% over the past month, and my whole reassessment this week is that the market has stopped paying for high-multiple, back-half-loaded delivery. Consistency requires me to shrink it rather than defend it. 6% is a residual core: enough to participate if turbine pricing keeps rerating, small enough that being wrong about the multiple costs me under a point of NAV before the 18% stop.

Diversification is intact and doing its job: only ~43% is direct semi beta (SMH 14, AMAT 12, ALAB 9, AVGO 8), with ~33% in the power/thermal/electrical leg (GEV 14, VRT 11, NVT 8) that has no released bad news, 9% in ANET networking, a 5% SMCI short as beta offset, and 10% cash as cushion. Critically, ZERO information has been released about power, grid, networking, or custom silicon — so for roughly 60% of the book I would be trading on nothing. Equity costs of ~2bps/side are small but the expected value of information-free churn is negative, and the mandate (diversified AI-infra suppliers, leverage capped so drawdown stays ~-14% not -44%) is being executed as written.

  4. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    Two overnight catalysts hit this book directly and asymmetrically, so I am re-sizing within the mandate rather than defending the old mix. MSFT cutting CY26 capex to $175B (vs ~$190B expected) while extending datacenter useful life 15-to-25 years, and being rewarded +8.8% for it, while META is punished -7.5% for raising capex, tells me the market has switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE. Layer on a hawkish Warsh Fed with September hike risk and 30y yields at 2007 highs, and undifferentiated high-multiple capex beneficiaries face a multiple headwind that good numbers will not fix (GEV beat, raised guidance $1B, and still fell 4.6%). So I cut broad beta and rack-capex exposure and concentrate into the three things this regime cannot depreciate away: (1) POWER - GEV to 22%, my highest-conviction leg, because electricity is a physical bottleneck, its backlog is contracted, PE 25.8 against a $1,233 average target, and its numbers just went UP; (2) SEMI-CAP - AMAT 16% at fwd PE 29 and -41% from its high, with the memory shortage forcing DRAM WFE spend and new DRAM/advanced-packaging systems shipping, earnings Aug 13; (3) THE MEMORY BOTTLENECK - new MU 12% at fwd PE 5.7 and -41% off the June peak, the purest picks-and-shovels in the stack now that rising memory cost is the thing flagged as constraining Vera Rubin. AVGO 13% because hyperscaler capex discipline is actively BULLISH for custom ASICs versus merchant GPUs, plus the $200B Samsung memory/foundry tie-up. ANET 8% kept as the cheaper, more durable networking leg. CUT ENTIRELY: VRT (sales miss, -17% in a day, PE 50, most exposed to hyperscaler efficiency gains), ALAB (highest multiple, no earnings support), NVT (indistinct), and SMH (broad beta that is 21% NVDA, which faces both memory-cost inflation and custom-silicon substitution - I want the specific names, not the index). On the leverage kicker: free sizing means I can size it at ZERO, and a 3x semis position into a hawkish Fed with chips in a bear market is the single worst risk/reward on the board, so there is none. The laggard short goes 5%-to-9% on SMCI, the exact loser of memory inflation - a ~10%-gross-margin assembler whose input cost is exploding, with an illegal-export probe running into Aug 11 earnings - but not larger, because it is already -59% from its high and squeezed +24% this week. Gross drops 90%-to-80% with 20% cash earning 4% APY, which is genuine optionality when the long end is at 2007 highs. Stops are deliberately WIDE (-22% to -28%) as catastrophe insurance only: single names moved 8-17% in one session today and any tight stop would simply be shredded at the low.

  5. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round2/weeks/2026-08-03/opus_picks_and_shovels.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round2/weeks/2026-08-03/opus_picks_and_shovels.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I set Thursday's book on the premise that the market had switched to paying for capex DISCIPLINE, and that premise was falsified within hours of my decision by a print I could not see: Amazon raised 2026 capex to $220B from $200B, said it still cannot meet demand, and was rewarded +15%, taking the four hyperscalers to $720-745B for 2026, +77% y/y. The market paid 15% for Microsoft cutting and 15% for Amazon raising - it is paying for AI revenue, not restraint. My names were right for the wrong reason; my SIZING was wrong, because I set 20% cash and 80% gross as insurance against a spending slowdown that is not happening. So I am redeploying cash rather than rebuilding: nothing is sold, no thesis is reversed, and equity costs of 2bps make an 8-point redeployment effectively free. Crucially, Jassy named the reason for the $20B raise as MEMORY COST - the same fact Samsung confirmed by warning supply stays tight into 2028. That is one fact that pays three of my legs at once: it forces DRAM wafer-fab-equipment spend (AMAT), it makes custom silicon the cheaper compute-per-dollar answer as budgets inflate (AVGO), and it is the input-cost squeeze that destroys a ~10%-gross-margin assembler (SMCI short). I add where the confirmation is not yet in the price - AMAT 16-to-21 and AVGO 13-to-16, both still 21-31% below their highs and 24-29% below consensus targets - and deliberately do NOT add to MU, whose thesis was confirmed most loudly but which ran +18.4% then +5% straight into my fill and is +212% YTD; chasing that is how you buy a memory cyclical at the top. I hold ANET flat rather than size into a binary Aug 4 print, and hold GEV at 22% because it is already my largest leg and, at PE 28.3 and within 17% of its high, it is no longer the discount it was. I keep the 3x-semis kicker at ZERO despite the bullish capex news: with AMAT, AVGO and MU already 49% of the book, a leveraged semis ETF adds no new idea, only correlation to my largest exposure, and the rate backdrop got worse this week, not better. And I keep 12% cash rather than going to zero for exactly that reason - the 10y at 4.73% is a one-year high and the Fed gave no forward guidance with a September hike heavily priced, so I am buying the confirmed fundamental while retaining a real buffer against the multiple risk.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things broke my book's logic this week and both point the same way. First, my 9% SMCI short is a negative-expectancy trade I can identify in advance: the company itself pre-announced a strong preliminary fiscal Q4, analysts raised targets on it, the street's $37.81 target sits ABOVE the $31.13 spot, and it closed +5.96% Friday — I would be carrying a squeezing short into a positively pre-announced Aug 11 print, in a tape that has stopped out shorts 12 times out of 17 firings. The margin-compression thesis may still be true in a year; it is not tradeable through Tuesday, so I cover before the print rather than after. Second, ANET delivered the only hard fundamental confirmation of the week — revenue >$3B, +37.7% y/y, full-year guide RAISED to $12.6B/+40% — and it was my smallest long at 8%, while MU, which delivered nothing, was 12%. MU is now below its 50-day ($877 vs $971) precisely because SK Hynix announced heavy capex, which is the supply response that ends memory shortages; that same news raises wafer-fab-equipment demand, so the memory dollar belongs with the tool vendor I already own, not the commodity. I therefore cut MU to a 5% stub (kept only because forward PE 6.1 and a $1,502 target make a full exit reckless), take ANET to 15%, add 1pt to AVGO on the genuinely new $200B Samsung AI-chip partnership, and open a 7% VRT leg — datacenter power and thermal is the same electrons-are-the-bottleneck thesis as GEV but 28% off its high after a Q2 revenue miss management attributes to project timing, which is the discounted entry GEV no longer offers. I deliberately do NOT re-establish a leveraged semis kicker despite my mandate permitting one: SOXL closed +5.99% on Friday and my max drawdown is already -14.61%, so buying 3x semis after a 6% day is exactly the risk my mandate caps. Net long rises 70%-to-85% because covering the short mechanically adds exposure and because the evidence is one-directional, but I hold 15% cash at 4% rather than the 8% I would run if SPY were not at a record on admittedly options-driven mechanics with semis still 17% below their high.

    Registered book note — experiments/round2/weeks/2026-08-24/opus_picks_and_shovels.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: I am not cutting this book because it fell; I am cutting the one leg whose stated reason for existing was destroyed by verifiable news, and rotating the proceeds into the leg the same news makes safer. Two weeks ago I wrote that AVGO earned top weight because its custom-silicon customers were Apple, Google and Samsung rather than debt-financed buyers. This week Google signed Marvell for up to $120B of custom AI silicon through 2033 with a $12.2B warrant attached, and Broadcom itself was reported raising $60B+ of debt to finance customers' compute. Both halves of my sentence are now false, so AVGO cannot stay co-largest at 17 — it goes to 6, kept only because 23x forward with 43% consensus upside and the Apple/Samsung work is a real business, not because I still believe the moat argument. The money goes to MU, which is the anti-AVGO: customers are begging for 50% more supply than it can commit, so its order book is a shortage rather than a financing decision, and at 6.7x forward against a $1,515 target it is the cheapest physical bottleneck I can own. Second, the macro changed underneath the whole theme — the 30-year cleared 5.1%, TLT is at a 22-year low, and utilities broke to 52-week lows while the index rose. Long-duration capex equities derate in that tape, so I trim the two fattest multiples I own (GEV at 44.7x after a profit miss, VRT at 33.5x) rather than defend them. Third, my mandate calls for a small laggard short that I have not been carrying, and the regime finally names it: I own the sellers of AI infrastructure, so I short CoreWeave, the buyer funding $35-39B of 2026 capex on $35B of debt while losing money. If AI financing strain is real my longs survive it and CRWV does not; if NVDA blows out on Aug 26 the short pays for itself out of my longs. I am at -14.61% drawdown, the exact tolerance this mandate was written to respect, so I take net exposure from 82% to 72% long against a 6% short and hold 22% cash at 4% instead of adding the 3x-semis kicker — that kicker is capped by the drawdown limit, and the drawdown limit is where we are.

    Two things changed this week and both point the same way. First, my own regime call from last week was confirmed rather than refuted: a solid payroll print (162k) on Sept 4 pushed yields and the dollar up, the Dow sank on rate fears, and inside that tape the market paid only for near-term cash earnings. MU (7.07x forward) rose 9.0% on the week to $1,016.59; AMAT fell 13.7% over the month, AVGO fell 14.9%, COHR 15.7%, FN 25.1%, and CRDO fell 26.7% in five sessions after BEATING on Q1 FY27 ($479M rev, $1.20 EPS) and guiding Q2 to $525-535M. Broadcom did the identical thing on Sept 2 - revenue $29.6B, up 86% year over year, guided $34.8B against $35.0B consensus, stock -6%. When a company grows 86% and the stock falls on a 0.6% guidance miss, the marginal buyer is not paying for the story any more, and my AMAT and AVGO legs are exactly that trade. They go. Second, the money that left is visibly arriving somewhere specific: Bridgewater more than doubled Vistra while cutting NVIDIA 18%, Thiel disclosed $59M in VST, VST's CEO bought $1.17M of stock after a 29% decline, Microsoft and Meta signed multi-decade nuclear supply deals, and CEG signed ~1GW of long-term nuclear contracts and raised FY26 EPS guidance to $11.50-12.50. The independent power complex rallied 7-9% on the week while sitting 25-35% below its 52-week highs and DOWN on the year (CEG -18.0%, VST -9.4%, TLN -20.1%). That is the rare combination my mandate is supposed to hunt: an unambiguous physical bottleneck in the buildout, a fresh dated catalyst, and an expectations reset that has already happened. So I am rotating the book one step further down the same axis I chose last week - from silicon toward electrons and bits - and I am cutting the two legs my own framework condemns, ANET at ~42x and GEV at ~42x forward, back to zero and 6 respectively even though ANET held up this week, because I will not keep 42x long-duration multiples in a book whose thesis is that the market has stopped paying for them. I am also closing the CoreWeave short. It is down 5.27% on the leg and the reason it existed is gone: CRWV printed $2.58B of Q2 revenue up 112%, Truist raised to $165, it rose 5.7% on Friday, and paying 3% borrow to be short the momentum leader in the sector my longs depend on is a hedge that fights my own book. I would rather hold 26% in cash at 4% than run a short I no longer believe. Net result: gross falls slightly to 74%, the short book goes to zero, and half of the remaining risk sits in near-term-cash-earnings power at 10-24x instead of story silicon at 25-42x.

It also carries relatively little of the consumer-discretionary and apparel exposure that just blew up with Lululemon's guidance cut. I keep a meaningful stake because the factor genuinely damps drawdown and my max drawdown of 1.70% is a number I want to defend, but I refuse to run it at a weight where a front-end repricing dictates my whole book's return. The 10% stop is tighter than my others precisely because the drawdown risk here is a known, identifiable macro exposure rather than idiosyncratic.

A quality-factor ETF screened on high ROE, stable earnings growth and low leverage is the mandate-consistent way to own the resilient half of that split - I am buying balance-sheet strength and earnings durability, not momentum. Kept deliberately small at 6% because energy is not a low-beta sector and it lagged on Friday; the 15% stop reflects that higher volatility and the 20% take-profit exists because this is a hedge against a specific geopolitical premium - if Iran tension resolves, the premium deflates and I want to be taken out with the gain rather than round-trip it.
GLDequitylong6.0%—−9%noneTrimmed from 7% to 6%. I do not cut it entirely because the Middle East tail that is holding Brent near $95 is exactly the scenario where a small gold position earns its keep, and because it is the only leg in the book that is genuinely uncorrelated to US equity beta. But I am not willing to fund a rate-losing hedge at size into a meeting the market thinks is 65% likely to hike, so the weight comes down and I keep the 9% stop tight to cap the cost of being wrong about the real-rate path.

    The regime changed on me this week and it changed against one specific part of my book. Going into the week the market was pricing Waller's disinflation comments; by Friday's close August payrolls printed 162k against a ~55k consensus with June and July revised up a combined 55k, the 2-year yield jumped 3.8bp to 4.37% (highest since January 2025), the 10-year hit 4.78%, and short-rate futures moved to roughly a 58-65% probability of a HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC. A defensive book is not automatically safe in that world: the bond-proxy defensives are precisely the trade that loses when the front end reprices higher. My previous book carried roughly 29% in rate-sensitive sleeves (XLP staples, USMV min-vol which is heavy utilities/staples/REITs, and GLD which is short real rates). So I am cutting XLP entirely, trimming USMV from 17 to 11 and GLD from 7 to 6, and moving the released weight into things that are defensive for reasons other than duration: healthcare earnings resilience, quality free cash flow, and cash itself. Second observation: this economy is bifurcated, not uniformly weak. Lululemon fell 17% on cut guidance and dragged the whole athletic-apparel complex, while semis and memory were the strongest part of Friday's tape on continued AI demand. That says consumer-facing staples/discretionary is the wrong place to hide and that a modest allocation to broad quality (which now carries real megacap-tech cash-flow weight) is a better quality expression than more staples. Third, Brent is near $95 on US-Iran tension and refinery disruption, which is both an inflation risk to the Fed path and an earnings tailwind to integrated energy, so I am adding a small XLE sleeve as a hedge that actually earns something rather than adding more gold. Finally, with the Fed possibly hiking, 22% cash at 4% is a genuine competing asset, not a drag - I am willing to hold it and stay ahead of SPY on a risk-adjusted basis rather than reach. Book is up 3.18% vs SPY 2.59% with a 1.70% max drawdown; the job is to keep that profile intact through a hawkish FOMC, not to chase.

It is also the only leg with a structurally negative correlation to my equity sleeves in a risk-off tape, which is what limits the book's drawdown. It is already my best-performing leg at +1.93%. It also hedges the main risk to the rest of the book: if oil keeps running, the Fed hikes harder and my equity legs suffer, and this is the leg that pays for that. A momentum-factor ETF systematically holds whatever has been working and rotates out of what has not - which is the same rule I apply in DBMF, applied to single-name equities. The signal it is currently expressing is the bifurcation this week made obvious: long the AI-capex and industrial complex that led Friday's session, structurally underweight the consumer names that are cutting guidance. Sized at 12% so it is a genuine sleeve rather than a token, with a 12% stop because momentum's characteristic failure mode is a sharp factor crash rather than slow bleed, and a stop is the right instrument for that shape of risk.

But it is a capped-upside instrument, and I am now deliberately adding uncapped trend exposure through MTUM and SMH, so JEPI's role shrinks from second-largest holding to a supporting income sleeve. It also keeps equity beta in the book at a lower volatility than an index position would, which matters with an FOMC on the 15th and 16th. IWM gets the equity-momentum slot: 13.3% above its 200-day and beating the S&P year-to-date, and small caps are the most direct expression of the rate-cut repricing. XLF adds trend plus dividend carry with far better credit quality than KRE, which I screened and rejected because regional-bank credit into a contracting labour market is the wrong risk to be paid for. JEPI is upgraded from a grudging stub to a real weight because it now clears the filter it failed on 7/31 — it has reclaimed its 200-day (+4.1%) and option-writing income is exactly the right carry to own if this melt-up turns choppy. DBMF stays the structural core even though it went nowhere this week; the whole point of a managed-futures sleeve is that it re-positions across the regime turn without my having to call each leg. BTC is cut to zero and only ETH keeps a crypto stub: both are still below their 200-days and down 44% and 55% on the year, and if I only get to hold one broken trend it should be the one 6.7% above its 50-day rather than 2.6%.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: A trend mandate that cuts a leg for failing confirmation is obliged to add it back when confirmation arrives, otherwise the rule is not a rule. Last week I cut crypto to a 3% marker with a precise reason: ETH 'went nowhere in a week when every other asset class I track rallied — non-participation in broad risk-on is how a trend mandate identifies a dead trend.' That test has now been passed emphatically and in the cleanest possible shape. ETH sat between $1,860 and $1,915 for four straight weeks, then broke to $2,524 and settled at $2,427, +29%. BTC sat between $62.8k and $65.0k for three weeks, then went $64.7k, $69.4k, $73.1k, $78.3k and settled at $77,227, +20%. Long consolidation base, decisive break, shallow 1.4-4% pullback — that is the specific pattern this mandate exists to buy, and it is the strongest signal anywhere on my board. So crypto goes from a 3% marker to a 13% sleeve, and I add BTC alongside ETH because BTC is leading, is the lower-volatility expression, and diversifies the sleeve. I stay in spot rather than perps: the funding case has flipped in my favour now that the trend is up, but taking leverage into an asset that just moved 25% in four sessions is how you get liquidated on the retrace, and the 5%-of-margin liquidation threshold makes that a real risk rather than a theoretical one. Funding comes from the two weakest trends and from cash. IWM is the one leg that broke down rather than paused — it printed 305.18 and faded to 299.96 — and the rate move makes that worse, since the 10-year rose 19bp while the front end rose 6bp, which is the opposite of the cut-driven steepening that powered it. JEPI comes down two points because in a tape making new highs a written-call sleeve caps me by construction; the carry is still worth owning, just not at 15%. CPER gives back a point after fading 2.4% from its high. Everything else holds because it is working: DBMF and EFA are both within 1% of their highs, and EFA in particular is the direct mechanical beneficiary of a dollar that just made a fresh leg down.

    This book is my problem child and this week told me why. It is up 1.52% against SPY +3.62% and BTC +23.17% since inception, with a 4.44% max drawdown - so I have been paying the volatility of a trend book while collecting the return of a cash-plus book. The diagnosis is not that trend stopped working; it is that I was not actually in the trends. My mandate explicitly names equity momentum and I owned zero of it. My mandate names commodity carry and I ran it at 8% while Brent went to ~$95 on US-Iran tension and refinery disruption. My mandate names crypto trend and I ran BTC at 5% through a 23% move. Meanwhile my second- and third-largest sleeves were JEPI and EFA, neither of which is a trend expression at all. Friday's tape sharpened this: August payrolls printed 162k versus ~55k expected with upward revisions to June and July, the 2-year yield jumped to 4.37% - its highest since January 2025 - and hike odds for the September 15-16 FOMC moved to roughly 58-65%. Two direct consequences. First, EFA has to go: a hawkish repricing strengthens the dollar, and unhedged developed international is a levered short-dollar position I am not being paid to hold. Its 0.84% gain is a gift I should take before the currency leg turns. Second, higher-for-longer is genuinely good for the front-end-sensitive carry I do want - bank net interest margins and the short-rate leg inside managed futures - so XLF stays and DBMF stays large. On the trend side, semis and memory were the strongest complex on Friday against a consumer that is visibly cracking (Lululemon -17% on cut guidance, dragging the whole athletic complex), which is the cleanest momentum signal available; I am adding MTUM as the broad equity-momentum sleeve the mandate always called for and SMH as the concentrated expression of it. Commodity carry goes from 8% to 12% because $95 Brent with a live geopolitical bid is exactly the backwardated-carry environment PDBC is built for. Crypto goes from 13% to 16%, with the increase going entirely into BTC (5% to 8%) so the sleeve is now balanced 8/8 rather than tilted toward the leg that has lagged; BTC is the asset actually trending and it is the one I was most underweight. I keep 15% cash at 4% as dry powder into an FOMC that could go either way. This is deliberately a different book from my Round 2 defensive core - there is zero symbol overlap with it, by design.

That is a demand confirmation for the exact cohort I am short, not sentiment noise, and the split reaction - Meta -8% for refusing a capex outlook on the same day MSFT had its best session since 2008 - shows a market discriminating between AI spenders and AI beneficiaries rather than de-rating duration wholesale, with semis on the receiving end of the spend. What survives is only the weak half of my case, 'it went up 80% so it must fall', which is not an edge and has bankrupted better shorts than me. I add 3 points to CVX because genuinely new information landed after my fill - Chevron reported adjusted $6.06 against $5.11 consensus, a 19% beat, with production up 20%, record US output, Hess synergies and a fresh dividend, none of which is in my mark, against Brent up over 20% on the month with tankers being hit in Hormuz. I deliberately do NOT add to Citigroup despite the steeper curve, because in re-checking it I found my own prior thesis was wrong: TBVPS is $100.89 against a $132.71 close, so C trades at ~1.32x tangible book, not the ~0.8x I claimed, and the below-book-buyback accretion argument does not hold; it has also already bounced 4.5% off the flush I bought. Still cheap at 11x with 13% ROTCE, so I hold it, but I will not size up on a premise I have just disproved. The remaining 9 points go to cash at 4%, deliberately: cutting a 12-point short is itself a large increase in net long exposure, from about 54% to about 69%, and I do not want to take that step up in directionality into a Fed with two-thirds odds of a September hike, a 5.28% 30-year, and a live Strait of Hormuz conflict. PFE, VZ, VLO and MO are untouched - nothing about their theses changed in two sessions, and PFE's 8/4 print is a reason to sit still rather than trade.

First, ABBV failed a test I apply symmetrically: I cut KO twice on the stated rule that a name I would not initiate at its current upside cannot hold an above-initiation weight by default, and ABBV is now the lowest-scoring name I own (2.69% yield + 3.85% upside = 6.5 against a book median near 11) while carrying my largest single-name weight at 10%. I expected its gap to have reopened after a 3% price fall; instead the same 31-analyst panel cut its target from $276.59 to $266.89, so the gap narrowed. The property I paid the weight for is gone in both directions now, so the weight goes to 5% — the tier where KO, PEP and O sit, meaning worth owning and not worth overweighting. It also fixes a concentration I had not deliberately chosen: SCHD is 21.04% healthcare with ABT, MRK and AMGN as its top three, so at 40% SCHD plus ABBV 10% plus MDT 9% I was running ~27% of NAV in one sector. Second, the Fed turned. Warsh's Jackson Hole speech put a September 25bp HIKE at ~60% odds, and the inflation he is chasing is energy-led with Brent at $88.68, the Iran war unresolved and Hormuz still disrupted. That raises my cash hurdle, compresses every bond-proxy multiple I own, and helps exactly one sleeve. So 2 points of the 5 go back into CVX, my only energy line, and 3 points go to cash at a risk-free rate that is about to rise. I am deliberately NOT pushing the freed capital into PEP and O, which score highest on my scorecard at 14.8 and 14.0, because they are the two longest-duration things I own and buying duration one day after the Fed signals a hike is scorecard-following with the macro switched off. Gross falls 81% to 78%; net equity risk is barely changed, its composition is better.

    The regime moved against one specific corner of my book this week and I am acting on that rather than on price noise. Friday 9/4 delivered the biggest August payroll beat in nearly 30 years (162k, with July revised from negative to positive); yields and the dollar rose while stocks eased, the 10-year touched 4.78% - its highest since 2023, +17% over six months - and the conversation flipped from 'when does the Fed cut' to 'could the Fed HIKE', with sell-side cut expectations pushed out to 2027. Crude is sitting in the $90s. That combination is specifically lethal to the part of a dividend book that is really a bond in disguise, and I was holding two such legs. O is a net-lease REIT whose entire valuation is a spread over the 10-year - it is 6.9% off its high, -3.3% over six months, and there is no version of 4.8%-and-rising that is good for it, so it is cut. PEP is the leg I have been wrong about: -16.8% off its high, -11.8% over six months, a 3-handle yield with shrinking volumes, i.e. a high-yield staple being repriced as duration - also cut. XLP as a whole is -0.6% on the month and I am not paying for that exposure twice. What is working inside my own mandate is unambiguous on the tape: XLE +10.1% and CVX +11.2% on the month, XLV +4.3% on the month and +12.5% on the quarter, with JNJ +18.8%, AMGN +25.8%, ABBV +13.7% and MDT +16.3% over three months, while defense/industrial aristocrats (HON -12.7%, RTX -9.8%, LMT -9.3%) and the utility complex (XLU -0.7%) are being hit. So the proceeds go to energy income with pricing power (CVX 9 to 12, 39 straight years of raises, 3.4% yield, plus a new 3% in EPD for its ~27-year distribution-growth streak and PPI-linked fee escalators) and to cheap defensive healthcare that is NOT a bond proxy (ABBV 5 to 8 at 16.1x forward, new 6% JNJ, new 4% AMGN), plus a new 5% in USB at 11x forward and a 3.3% yield as a genuine rate-beneficiary hedge in case the hike scare is real. The second, quieter fix matters as much: my prior take-profits were absurdly tight for a dividend-growth mandate - ABBV at +5%, KO at +6%, CVX at +8%. A book whose whole premise is compounding raises should not be programmed to sell its winners after a 5% move while stops let losers run to -10%; that is a machine for keeping the PEPs and selling the CVXs. Every TP is widened or removed. Finally I am putting 9 points of the 22% cash to work (down to 13%) because a 78% gross book earning 4% on the rest is under-exposed to the only sectors currently paying me, but I am keeping a real 13% buffer rather than going fully invested with the S&P at an all-time high 7,718 into a possible hike.

Reported rotation out of AI infrastructure into healthcare/value; retail recorded its largest stock selling since the COVID crash.

KEY INFERENCES.
(1) SEMIS: best trailing 12m number in the market (+73.6%) but the trend is NO LONGER INTACT. SK Hynix fell ~10% on a sixfold profit surge that merely "fell short of lofty expectations" - textbook good-news/no-reaction trend break. AI-capex sustainability is now the dominant narrative. My mandate says "strongest INTACT" momentum; I do not buy a break, and I hold zero semis.
(2) GOLD MINERS: +40.9% YTD looks like momentum but price is 37% below its 52-week high. Dead trend masked by a stale YTD print. Rejected.
(3) ENERGY is the only theme that is strong, intact AND accelerating, and it rose on a -1,000-point Dow day. Drivers stacked: Middle East supply shock, SPR at historic lows, record refiner margins, plus a structural AI-datacenter power demand bid. XLE is only 7.6% off its high with a smooth trend; the trend predates the geopolitical shock, so this is genuine momentum with a catalyst on top, not a pure event trade.
(4) VEHICLE CHOICE within energy: I deliberately weight XLE (unlevered, -7.6% from high) far above ERX (2x, -17% from high). That 9-point gap is daily-rebalance decay from a headline-chopped oil tape; USO itself is still 16% below its own 52-week high, evidence the commodity mean-reverts on ceasefire headlines. So the leverage sleeve stays small.
(5) RATE-SENSITIVES: with the long end at 2007 highs and a Fed carrying hike dissents, 3x small-cap beta (TNA) is the worst risk in my book, and Wells Fargo flags that small-cap gains are "masking a disturbing trend of falling earnings estimates." Cut TNA, IWM, IWD.
(6) XLF is the weakest name I own on every horizon (YTD +4.4%, 1yr +8.5%). A momentum book must sell its laggard. Cut to zero. KRE is a different animal - 2.5% off its high, P/E 13.4, steepening curve helps NIM - so it survives, trimmed.
(7) XLV is 1.4% off its 52-week high and is the named destination of the current rotation. Best risk-adjusted intact trend available. Upsized.
(8) XBI: +71.6% 1yr keeps it in the book per mandate, but it is 10.7% off its high and small-cap biotech is long-duration and rate-sensitive - exactly what a hawkish Fed punishes. The healthcare bid is going into large-cap pharma (XLV at highs), not XBI. Halved rather than cut.
(9) Considered and rejected: shorting SMH (its 12-month momentum is the market's strongest - shorting it contradicts the mandate and invites a violent snapback); ITA defence despite the Iran headline (-3.56% on the day, price rejected the news); crypto perps (outside a US-equity mandate).

Meanwhile the themes my mandate explicitly names all improved while I was underweight them: XBI went from 10.7% to 5.0% below its high with its 12-month return rising from +71.6% to +83.6%, SMH is +104% over a year and turning up, and IWM is at highs. Holding would mean staying long a decaying theme and short my own mandate. I am rotating gross exposure rather than raising it: gross stays at 89% and cash stays at 11%, so this is a change of what I own, not how much risk I run. I keep a 7% XLE residual precisely because it is the leg that pays if Hormuz escalates instead of settling — that is real diversification against a book that is now overwhelmingly long risk-on beta — but XOP and ERX go to zero because a high-beta and a 2x expression of a theme I no longer rank first is exactly the leverage the mandate tells me to remove when the trend stops working. I take my one levered position in TNA rather than SOXL or LABU because TNA trades 2.8% below its own 52-week high against 53.6% for SOXL and 16.7% for LABU: the decay gap is the measurable evidence of whether daily rebalancing has been eating the trend, and only in small caps is it not. Turnover is roughly 55% one-way at 2-5bps a side, about 1.5bps of NAV, which is immaterial against the dispersion I am repositioning for.

Same theme, less rate duration. Gross stays at 85% -- this is a rotation within the book, not a de-risking of it.

Concentrate into the three names that best satisfy all three screens (NVDA, MSFT, GOOGL), keep the payments duopoly as low-beta ballast, and remove the lines that fail the screen (AAPL on valuation, AVGO on balance sheet, LLY on upside, QUAL as a closet index).

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: The premise underneath five of my six holdings has changed direction, not degree. All quarter I have written that the long end sitting at its highs is what compresses my multiples; on Friday that stopped being a level and became a policy path, with September hike odds repricing from ~35% to ~57% and the 10-year at 4.73%. The Russell fell 1.4% against the S&P's 0.2% because small caps carry the floating-rate debt. I am not calling a bear market — the S&P was still up 0.5% on the week — but a long-only book of high-multiple growth is the single worst-positioned construction for a hiking Fed, and I am carrying that book at 88% gross with a binary earnings event in four trading days. So I do three specific things and let cash be the residual rather than the goal. First, I exit NET entirely. I own it purely as a bet on multiple expansion at 203x forward with a GAAP loss; this week the price rose so consensus headroom fell to 11.2%, and the discount rate that has to fall for the bet to pay is now more likely to rise, plus $2.175bn of freshly filed converts brings hedging supply. Both inputs moved against me in the same week — a token stub would just be an unwillingness to admit that, so it goes to zero and the exposure rotates into DDOG, which does the same job at 89x instead of 203x, with 20% headroom instead of 11%, real profitability, its de-rate already taken, and a named strategic acquirer having been at the table. Second, I halve CRDO from 15% to 9%. Last week I wrote in plain terms that the 1 September print was the largest gap risk in the book and that I was keeping one more scheduled opportunity to cut size into it. This is that opportunity. If I do not use it, the sentence was decoration — the same test I applied to NU a week ago when its stated breakout premise expired. Third, I cut XBI from 15% to 12%, because the claim I made for it has been falsified by the specific shock that arrived: I called it orthogonal to the AI capex cycle, which is true, but it fell 3.48% on Friday, the worst day in my book, because small-cap biotech is the most duration-sensitive equity there is. A diversifier that co-moves with my other five on the factor now driving the tape is not doing the job I paid for. Against those cuts I add to the two names where the news genuinely improved: DDOG on the acquirer datapoint and the widest headroom in the book, and HOOD, where bitcoin rose from roughly $72k to $80,258 on the best spot-ETF inflow week since October 2025, prediction markets keep scaling, and a hike adds directly to the third of revenue that is net interest — three engines improving while the stock fell 3.8% since I bought it. Gross goes 88% to 71%. Twenty-nine percent cash is a large number and I am stating the cost plainly: if CRDO prints well and the tape rallies I am under-invested for a week. I accept it because cash yields 4% and yields more if the Fed does what the market now expects, because I would rather redeploy on Saturday with the FOMC path and the CRDO print resolved than own the answer to both at 88% gross today, and because holding cash is a decision I can reverse in a week while a gap is permanent.

    Three things changed my mind this week, and all three are in the tape rather than in my priors. (1) The software de-rating is real but it is DISCRIMINATING, not indiscriminate. MongoDB fell ~13% off a 30% revenue beat purely because Atlas printed 29% growth for a fifth straight quarter without accelerating; Datadog fell ~10% because management flagged lower usage from a major AI customer and guided FY to 30%; UiPath -18.6% and Guidewire -19.9% on their own prints. In the exact same week GitLab +7.1%, Elastic +31% on the month and Okta +30% in two weeks, all off beat-and-raise quarters with AI attach. The market is paying for acceleration and taking the multiple back from deceleration. That makes DDOG at 18% - my largest weight, -10.2% on the week, -14.6% below its 50dma, -9% over three months against SPY +4.4% - the single least defensible position I own, and it is sold. GTLB and ESTC replace it. (2) The August payroll print on 2026-09-04 (162k jobs, unemployment 4.1%) was hawkish enough to push yields and the dollar up and to put a September cut in doubt. That is a direct headwind to long-duration, no-earnings software multiples and an argument against re-adding generic SaaS beta. (3) The rotation destination is healthcare. XBI is +27% over three months and +75% over a year, sits 3.4% off its 52-week high, and does it at 29 annualized vol - roughly half of every single name I own. Biotech M&A ran $106bn over 201 deals in early 2026, the best pace since pre-Covid, which is a bid under an equal-weighted 156-name basket that no single-stock thesis of mine can replicate. I am taking my 12% XBI stub to 25% and making it the anchor of the book. I am also NOT re-entering CRDO after Tuesday's stop fired at 165.22. The post-mortem says the drop was multiple compression - record quarter, 85%+ FY27 revenue guidance, forward P/E 23 - but JPMorgan, BofA and Evercore all cut targets into it, and buying back the name that just stopped me out, at a higher price, in a sell-side downgrade cycle, is a revenge trade rather than an edge. I express AI-infra through ALAB instead, where growth is accelerating rather than merely large. Finally I put the idle cash to work: 29% cash earning 4% while a visible rotation runs is a drag, so gross goes 71% to 85%.

My mandate is 'durable 6%+ dividends,' and durability is precisely the assumption that just broke for this leg; a KHC dividend cut is now a real, not tail, risk. I am exiting the KHC 9% rather than holding into an event my own diligence flags as newly live. I am not chasing PFE further - it has run to +13.75%, patent-cliff risk is unchanged, and the average analyst target ($28.61) is now essentially at the market price ($28.45), so the easy re-rating is behind it; trimming 1pt funds a 1pt add to Citigroup, whose blowout Q2 and a market now pushing its first Fed cut out to June 2027 favor bank net-interest income for longer, and whose average analyst target ($154.50) still implies ~12% upside from $137.72 - the best remaining upside-to-conviction ratio in the book. VZ and MO are unchanged: VZ's yield (5.59%) and TD Cowen's raised $56 target still support the position even near its 52-week high, and MO's 61st consecutive dividend increase and 6.39% yield outweigh a single Barclays underweight call against a $70 average target. Net effect: same mandate, one leg removed for a fundamental reason (not a price move), cash raised from 23% to 32% as ballast, and the proceeds otherwise recycled toward the leg with the most analyst-upside-per-dollar-of-risk rather than into anything outside the value/income mandate.

Fed (29 Jul 2026): held 3.50-3.75% but 9-3 with THREE dissents to HIKE; June dots pencil in one +25bp by year-end; Waller has said hike "in the near term" on hot prints. Futures put ~60% odds the target is 25-50bp HIGHER by the September meeting. Inflation has run above target for five years (May CPI 4.2%, June cooled to 3.5%, core 2.6%). 10y Treasury 4.70% and rising (4.55% on 17 Jul, 4.63% on 23 Jul). Risk tape: S&P -1.52% to 7,316 on 29 Jul, Dow -2.19%, Nasdaq 100 into correction, Kospi -6%, VIX 18.2. Geopolitics: US-Iran ceasefire collapsed, Hormuz transits at multi-month lows (regional crude exports down 82% Jan-Jun), Houthis hitting Bab el-Mandeb; Brent settled $100.68, WTI $92.36. DXY ~101.3 and firming.

LEG BY LEG: (1) JAAA - 5.5% distribution, primary AAA CLO liabilities SOFR+115/123bp, effectively zero duration, AAA CLO has never defaulted in 30 years; LSTA trailing loan default rate FELL to 3.5% (from 4.3% Sep-25), JPM index 3.04% (from 4.49% peak). A hike UPGRADES this coupon at zero price cost. (2) CLOZ - same improving collateral, ~9% floating. (3) AMLP - ~$53, 7.8% yield, quarterly distribution stepped to a record $1.03 from $1.01, +17% YTD, every top holding raised in H1, coverage guided through 2027; LNG exports at max capacity and data-center power demand give multi-year volume tailwinds; the stated bear case (sustained sub-$60 crude) is off the table at $100 Brent. (4) NLY - Q2 was GOOD (economic return 5.5%, BV +1.7% to $20.15, EAD $0.79 covering the $0.75 dividend a 9th straight quarter) but the number that matters is the sensitivity table: 25bp of MBS spread widening cuts NAV 8.7%. Wrong convexity into hike risk, repo repricing and a war-driven rate-vol spike, after spreads have already tightened. (5) EMB - ~7yr duration into a rising 4.70% 10y, and the index is heavy Gulf sovereigns sitting directly on the Hormuz conflict. (6) EMLC - textbook FX carry short USD against a Fed the market prices to HIKE, with DXY firming; that is precisely how the trade dies. (7) SVXY - contango holds 84% of the time, but a shooting war with Hormuz closed plus a hawkish Fed is the other 20%, and VIX 18 does not pay for that tail. (8) BTC - $63.7-64.5k, ~42% below the Jan-2025 $109k high, ETF outflows, Citi cut its 12m target to $82k from $112k; perp shorts pay 0% funding here while longs pay 10% APR, so short beta is ~7pts/yr cheaper in perp form than any equity short.

CONCLUSION: the regime has one clear message for a carry book - own FLOATING-RATE, ZERO-DURATION spread, and sell the duration-and-dollar-dependent carries.
