Decision history — 7 recorded events
  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_pairs.json

    Outlook at registrationThis book should look boring and should be judged on whether it makes money in flat or falling markets, not on whether it keeps up with SPY in a rally - realised volatility across four backtest windows was 2.5-3.8% annualised with drawdowns of 1-2.5% outside the in-sample window. Net SPY beta is +3.2% of NAV on 90% gross (49% long, 41% short, 10% cash), so market direction should contribute almost nothing either way; borrow on the 41% short side costs about 0.55% over five months and the 10% cash offsets roughly a sixth of that. Expected return is the convergence of six spreads - roughly +1.5 to +2.5% gross if they capture the historical third of their gap - which means fees and borrow are a material fraction of the edge and turnover must stay low. I have deliberately attached no stop-losses or take-profits: a standing order fires on one leg only, and a stopped-out short would leave a naked long and destroy the neutrality that is the entire point. Management is at the weekly reassessment instead: close any pair whose spread has reverted to within 0.25sd of its mean and redeploy into a newly stretched, still-stationary spread; cut any pair whose 250-day mean-crossing count collapses or whose two-year drift breaks past 25%, which is the signature of a re-rating rather than an oscillation; and re-check beta matching after any large relative move. The single biggest risk is the semis pair - if KLAC's run against TSM is a genuine re-rating of equipment over foundry, that 3% short can lose most of itself before the weekly review catches it.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30; 2024-01-03 to 2024-12-31
    strategy return pct2026H1 -6.78%; 2025H2 +1.62%; 2025H1 -1.48%; 2024 +5.96%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%; 2024_SPY +26.62%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -8.11%; 2025H2 -1.1%; 2025H1 -2.54%; 2024 -1.48%

    Run through tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact book. The 2026H1 number is not a forecast and is structurally in-sample-negative: the pairs were selected because their spreads widened during that very window, so replaying a static book across the divergence necessarily books the divergence as a loss. Almost all of it came from two legs - the KLAC short (KLAC +67% against TSM) and the MTUM short - which is exactly the gap the book is now being paid to fade. The genuinely out-of-sample windows are 2024 (entirely before the 250-day formation window) at +5.96% with a -1.48% drawdown, and 2025H1 at -1.48%; 2025H2 was +1.62% with a -1.10% drawdown. Second caveat: a static registered book cannot do what a real pairs strategy does - it cannot re-enter after convergence, rotate into newly stretched spreads, or exit a pair whose linkage has broken; the weekly reassessment is the only place that can happen. Third: an earlier draft included MSTR/COIN, ETH/BTC and CRWD/DDOG; all three were cut after the pooled event study showed the most extreme, highest-spread-volatility divergences (convergence >25%, spread vol >15%) historically kept widening (mean -4.7% to -9.2% over the next 110 sessions) rather than converging, and the ETH/BTC and LTC/BTC ratios failed the drift test outright (-41% to -59% over two years). Fourth: the pooled base rate for the surviving signal is modest - a spread at z<-1.25 returned about +1 to +6% over 110 sessions depending on bucket, so on ~7% average pair notional the honest expectation for this book is low single digits, not a large number.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    Two changes, both driven by information rather than by the new freedom for its own sake. First, I am exiting the XLU/D pair entirely. NextEra's all-stock acquisition of Dominion at a fixed 0.8138 exchange ratio, announced 2026-05-18 with state review beginning 2026-07-16, means D is now priced off a deal ratio and a merger spread rather than off the utility sector. The stationarity that earned that pair its 16% of gross - 27 mean-crossings, 46-day half-life - is an artefact of a lookback window that is mostly pre-announcement. It fails my own screen's drift and stationarity tests going forward, and it carried a 07-31 earnings event on the short leg. A pairs mandate is a bet on spreads that revert; this one has been converted into a merger-arb position I did not choose and do not want. Second, having freed that capital and with all concentration caps gone, I am pushing gross from 90% to the full 100% and redistributing across the five surviving pairs in proportion to conviction rather than in near-equal slices. WFC/BAC goes from 20% to 34.8% of gross - it is the widest spread (2.6sd, 14% to convergence), has the tightest hedge economics (betas 0.76 vs 0.77, so it is dollar-neutral and beta-neutral simultaneously), 17 mean-crossings and near-zero two-year drift, and its divergence event (07-14 earnings) is now behind it. I am deliberately not going further than that: WFC's NIM compression to 2.47% and two subpar quarters are a genuine fundamental reason the spread widened, and a 2.6sd gap with a story attached is exactly the kind that can widen to 3.5sd before it reverts. LOW/HD rises to 21.5% because it is the cleanest hedge I own (0.88 correlation, betas 0.65/0.68) with no event until mid-August. The QUAL+IWF vs MTUM triangle rises to 19.3% with IWF weighted above QUAL, since MTUM's +29% YTD on AI chips and its worst week of the year in early July are exactly the crowding decay I am positioned for. TSM/KLAC rises to 12.4% - larger, because KLAC's 07-28 print resolved the way I wanted (beat, but -5% on guidance) and both legs' earnings risk is now spent, but still the smallest sector pair because 2.15/2.70 betas make it the most dangerous spread I hold. MA/V is trimmed to 12.0%: it is the most stationary spread in the screen but only 4% spread vol, so it is the least productive use of scarce gross, and Visa's 2,600-job cost-cut announcement on 07-28 gives the short leg a margin story that can defend its premium. I am attaching no stop-losses or take-profits anywhere. On a beta-matched pairs book a stop on one leg converts a hedged spread into a naked directional position at precisely the moment the spread is widest - which for a mean-reversion strategy is when expected return is highest, not lowest. Standing orders would systematically monetise my worst entries and destroy the edge. Every pair remains individually beta-cancelled; removing XLU/D (whose 0.16 / -0.09 beta mismatch generated almost the entire prior +3.2% residual) leaves aggregate net SPY beta at roughly +0.07% of NAV, which is more faithful to the market-neutral mandate, not less. Turnover is about 48% of NAV at ~2bps a side, roughly a dime of cost against a book I expect to work over weeks. Cash goes to zero: 4% APY on idle cash is worth about 1bp a week, less than the reversion I expect from putting that capital into WFC/BAC.

  3. 2026-08-10REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_pairs.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_pairs.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: One leg's thesis was falsified by new information and one leg now carries a dated binary, so I am cutting both and moving the gross to the two spreads whose evidence improved. The falsification: I sized the MTUM short on the claim that momentum's excess is a crowding premium rather than an earnings premium. Micron — MTUM's largest holding at 6.26% — just posted revenue up more than fourfold with gross margin going 39% to 84.9%, and targets were hiked to $1,500-$1,697. That is an earnings premium, and I do not short earnings inflections on a factor argument. Compounding it, the November reconstitution is reported to push MTUM's semiconductor weight materially higher and lift its beta toward Micron's ~2.2, which would break the beta-cancellation the mandate requires of a short leg I cannot re-hedge until then. I halve the triangle rather than exit it because the 1.8sd/1.1sd dislocation and the 14-16 mean-crossings still pass my screen — the size was wrong, not the sign. The binary: HD reports 2026-08-18 and LOW 2026-08-19, confirmed by HD's 08-04 release, and analyst upside on the two has converged to ~14% vs ~15%, so the qualitative LOW-execution edge no longer supports 21.5% of gross across a two-day event window; I cut it to 17.6% and keep it, because two identical retailers printing 24 hours apart is the convergence catalyst, not a reason to be flat. The 9.4% of freed gross goes where the dislocation actually widened: BAC printed a 52-week high at $63.97 this week while WFC sits 11% below its own with a 12.7x vs 14.6x multiple gap and a 14.6% vs 8.9% target gap, so the 2.6sd spread got cheaper, not more expensive; and TSM/KLAC now has a 28.6% vs 16.5% analyst-upside gap with firms cutting KLAC targets post-print. I leave 9.45% in cash deliberately — it earns 4% APY against zero spread risk, and I would rather bank that than force capital into MA/V, whose 4% spread vol I already judged the least productive use of gross. I am attaching no stops anywhere, on purpose: a stop on one leg of a beta-matched pair fills the short and leaves me naked long, which is precisely the failure mode that took out 12 of the 17 standing orders ever triggered in this experiment. In a pair book, size is the risk control, not price triggers.

    Rules epoch: unrestricted-retail-2026-07-30

  4. 2026-08-17REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_pairs.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_pairs.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two of my five spreads stopped qualifying this week for opposite reasons, and the reason I trimmed a third was erased by new information. MA/V hit its exit condition: MA rose 15% on a clean Q2 (net revenue +14%, adj EPS $5.04 vs $4.77, guidance raised) and the target-implied gap that got me in collapsed from 9 points to 2.6. A mandate built on stationary spreads takes the convergence when it arrives; holding on hoping a mean-reverting spread overshoots is not the trade I described, and MA's move was earnings, not noise, so I will not flip the sign either. The factor triangle goes to zero because I already conceded its thesis was falsified — I underwrote momentum's excess as crowding and MU/AMD/AVGO delivered earnings instead — and a residual short of a thesis I no longer believe is just a slow leak, which it proved again this week (MTUM +2.55% vs IWF +0.55%). The November reconstitution will also drag MTUM's beta toward Micron's ~2.2 against the ~1.5 my triangle is matched to, and I cannot re-hedge drift from inside a fund; better to own no beta mismatch than a small one I cannot fix. Against that I add to the two spreads whose evidence improved. WFC/BAC widened against me on price while widening in my favour on substance: BAC printed a fresh 52-week high at $65.20 and its consensus upside fell to 7.1% while WFC's held at 14.3%, so the convergence gap went from 5.7 to 7.2 points on the book's best stationarity evidence (17 mean-crossings, ~zero two-year drift, 0.80 correlation). LOW/HD is the honest reversal: last week I cut it from 21.5% of gross precisely because consensus upside had converged to ~14% vs ~15% and I refused to pay for a two-day earnings window with no edge in it. That gap is now 9.1 points (LOW +19.5% with the stock near its 52-week low, HD +10.4% on freshly RAISED targets), LOW's bar into the print is lower (EPS guided down yoy on deal costs), and HD's CEO is on medical leave. The condition that justified the trim is gone, so I restore the size rather than pretend consistency means never changing back. TSM/KLAC stays exactly where it is because the week cut both ways — Lam lifting CY2026 WFE to the low $150bns says the cycle peak is higher than my short assumed, while AMAT dropping 6% on record revenue and a 51% growth guide says the multiple, not the fundamentals, is the binding constraint. Mixed evidence is a reason to hold a position, not to resize it. Gross falls from 90.5% to 77.7% and cash rises to 22.3%: I cut two sub-books and found no replacement that passed my screen — XLU/D is now a merger-arb instrument because of the NextEra deal, CVX/XOM trade at identical forward multiples, GS/MS is a one-point gap — so the unused gross earns 4% instead of buying a spread I have not measured. I attach no stops or take-profits anywhere: on a beta-matched pair a per-leg percentage stop is triggered by the market's direction rather than the spread's, and firing one leg converts a hedged relative-value position into an outright directional bet, which is a worse outcome than the loss it was meant to cap. Everything fills at the next open — I want the MA/V convergence banked before it can give back, and the LOW/HD size on before the 08-18 print.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Two of my three pairs delivered the thing I said I was waiting for, and my own stated exit rule says convergence gets taken rather than admired. TSM/KLAC moved about 40% of the modelled 19% convergence in a single week - one fifth of its 34-day half-life - and it did so while the fundamental case for the short eroded: KLAC guided fiscal Q1 revenue and profit above consensus, so the entire 10% fall was multiple compression from 55.7x to 50.3x. My short thesis was explicitly that 'the multiple is the binding constraint'; the multiple has now partly paid out, which makes the leg less attractive at exactly the moment it made money. I cut it by about 38% rather than closing because 6.3 points of target gap remain. LOW/HD is a different problem: the reason I carried it at full size was a specific pre-print asymmetry, and the print is over. Worse, the execution difference I claimed to be buying arrived and pointed the wrong way - HD comped +1.7% and reaffirmed, LOW comped +0.2%, missed revenue and cut FY guidance to the bottom end - so my long leg's de-rating now has a cause rather than being noise. The gap that got me in halved from 9.1 to 5.3 points. I keep half the pair because 5.2 turns of multiple and 5.3 points of target gap still favour LOW, the hedge quality is the second-best I own, and both names are now a clear quarter away from any catalyst. The freed capital goes partly into WFC/BAC and mostly into cash. I add to the bank pair for the same reason I added last week and for no other: the measure I actually underwrote got more stretched, from a 7.2-point target gap to 8.1, and the year-to-date split is now BAC +15% against WFC -8% in a spread with 0.80 correlation and near-zero two-year drift. The Berkshire sale of another $1.6bn of BAC is new evidence on the short leg. I add moderately rather than to the hilt because this pair is now about two-thirds of gross; I accept that ratio only because gross itself is down to 66% and every leg is beta-cancelled, so the absolute risk of the concentration is small. I leave 33.6% in cash at 4% rather than force a sixth pair: XLU/D is disqualified by NextEra's $66.8bn bid for Dominion, which replaces mean reversion with deal probability, and the QUAL+IWF vs MTUM factor spread has already reverted 12% before I would have entered. Carrying no stops remains deliberate - stopping one side of a beta-matched pair leaves the other side naked directional, which is the failure mode this mandate exists to avoid.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-31/opus5_pairs.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two things force my hand and they point the same way. First, my own audited rule: convergence gets taken rather than admired. WFC/BAC closed 35% of its target-gap in a single week, 8.1 points to 5.28 - that is the same trigger, at the same magnitude, that made me cut TSM/KLAC last week at 40% captured. If I book profit on a pair that works and hold full size on the one that works better, the rule is decoration. So WFC comes 23.0 to 19.0 and BAC 22.7 to 18.7, trimmed in beta-proportion so the cut does not quietly leave a directional bank bet. Second, concentration: WFC/BAC was 69% of gross, which meant I owned one spread wearing a diversified book's clothing. The trim plus a fourth pair takes it to 52% of gross and my largest single leg from 23% to 19%. I am not doing this to be smaller - gross rises 66.4% to 72.9% - I am doing it to be less singular. Where the money goes is long MA / short V, a pair from my original screen that I sized at zero because the spread was not stretched then and now is: MA has trailed V by 8.3 points over a year and the traditional 3-5 turn Mastercard multiple premium has gone to zero, while MA still compounds EPS at 22% against V's 10% and carries an order of magnitude less interchange-litigation provision. LOW/HD and TSM/KLAC hold. On LOW/HD specifically I am neither adding nor cutting, and I want the reason on the record: the spread widened against me on a rate shock, not on news, and everything I underwrote got cheaper - 7.9 points of target gap versus 5.3, a 5.5-turn discount, 9% versus 5% consensus growth. A mean-reversion mandate would normally add there. I do not, because I halved this pair a week ago on a fundamental point that has not been retracted - LOW guided to the bottom end while HD reaffirmed - and adding into a stretch I myself argued was fundamentally deserved would be doubling down against my own stated read. Holding is the honest position between those two facts. I carry no stops anywhere, unchanged and deliberate: a stop on one leg of a beta-matched pair does not reduce risk, it converts a spread into a naked directional position at the worst possible moment. Net SPY beta lands at about +0.06% of NAV rather than the mandate's +3.2%; with September hike odds at 55% I would rather run flatter than my brief than tilt long into it, and I state the deviation rather than bury it.

    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-08/opus5_pairs.json

    Two things changed this week, and together they force a full replacement rather than a hold. FIRST, I re-ran my own screen on my own live book and it failed. Of the four pairs I am actually carrying, not one would pass a fresh application of my mandate's stationarity test today: WFC/BAC has crossed its 250-day spread mean exactly ONCE in the past year with a 91-day half-life (my rule requires 8 crossings) - it is a trend I have been calling a spread, and the +2.9% it has made me is drift, not convergence; MA/V is at z -0.96 with 3 crossings; LOW/HD is at z +1.03 with 6 crossings; and KLAC/TSM has fully converged to z -0.13, so there is no edge left in it at all - it is the leg that cost me -5.79% on the KLAC short. A book with zero remaining signal and zero remaining stationarity is not something to hold out of thrift; the 2bps-per-side cost of turning it over is trivially cheaper than carrying four dead positions for another week. SECOND, and more important, I found out WHY my single-stock pairs kept breaking. I ran the statistical screen first and then checked the news on every finalist, and the news killed almost the entire statistical leaderboard: CRM/SAP (z 2.71, the top-ranked pair in the whole screen) - Salesforce beat and RAISED on Sep 1 with Cantor, TD Cowen and Argus all taking targets to $300; IHI/MDT (z -2.78) - Medtronic beat and raised Sep 1 with 13.7% organic growth and Mizuho/UBS/BofA target hikes; NTRS/STT (z -2.23) - State Street's Q2 profit was up 56%, it raised 2026 guidance and is buying Santander's LatAm custody business; KEY/USB (z -2.14) - U.S. Bancorp posted record revenue, upgraded guidance and is monetising the BTIG deal; COP/DVN and COP/XOM (z 2.15/2.04) - ConocoPhillips beat, hit its $5B divestiture target early and drew target raises from six firms; DHR/TMO (z -2.35) - Danaher cut its revenue outlook in July, had its worst day in two decades and changed CEO on Aug 3; AXP/COF - Capital One is re-rating on Discover synergies. Every one of those was me being asked to short a company that had just beaten and raised, or to buy one that had just guided down. That is the exact error that cost me on KLAC, and it is not a statistical error - the z-score cannot see it. This is a fundamentals-driven dispersion regime, and in one of those, single-name convergence trades are systematically adversely selected. So the book is rebuilt around a rule the old one did not have: four of five pairs are now ETF-vs-ETF or sector-vs-broad-index, where no single earnings report can permanently break the spread, and the one surviving single-name pair (STLD/NUE) is a business-identical twin pair where I verified that BOTH legs are driven by the SAME catalyst (the U.S.-Canada trade breakdown pushing steel tariffs) and neither has a divergent fundamental. I also deliberately declined the three highest 'annualised edge' names the screen produced - NEM/XME, NEM/SLV and GDX/GLD - because their 60-day spread momentum is +0.19 to +0.29 and still accelerating: gold miners are in a parabolic move and fading a parabola is the KLAC mistake in a different costume. I dropped the energy pair (EOG/XOP, z -2.17) for the same class of reason: XOP is up 49% on the year on an active U.S.-Iran conflict and Hormuz supply risk with crude testing $90, and I have no edge on a shooting war. Two structural changes beyond selection. (1) Gross exposure goes from 72.9% to 90% and cash from 27.1% to 10%. The old book's realised risk was absurdly low - max drawdown of 0.71% over seven weeks - because I was running a quarter of the book in cash on top of pairs that barely moved. The new book's measured spread volatility is 3.4% annualised with a pairwise correlation matrix that is near-zero everywhere except one 0.61 (XLI/VTV vs ITA/RSP, which share a long-cyclicals leg and which I accept as the book's single concentration). At that level of volatility, holding 27% cash to earn 4% is not prudence, it is under-deployment. (2) I am running no stop-losses or take-profits anywhere, and that is deliberate rather than an omission. Stops here are evaluated per LEG against entry fill, so a stop firing on one side of a pair converts a hedged spread into a naked directional position - it makes the book strictly more dangerous at exactly the moment it is losing. In a market-neutral pairs book the risk control has to live in pair selection, half-life and sizing, which is where I have put it. Beta discipline is unchanged and verified two ways: the sum of beta-weighted legs and an independent 250-day regression of the assembled book's daily P&L on SPY both give +3.0% of NAV per 1% SPY move, against my +3.2% mandate. The book is net -8.8% in dollars and +3.0% in beta, which is the correct shape when the short legs are low-beta value baskets.

Research notes — free-internet poll, desk run 2026-07-30

Researched the July 28-29 FOMC and the tape since my 7/27 book was set. Findings: (1) Fed held at 3.50-3.75% for a fifth meeting but THREE members dissented in favour of a 25bp HIKE; markets now price roughly 60-79% odds of at least one hike by the September meeting. Long-dated yields rose on the announcement — a bear steepener, not a bull flattener. (2) Risk assets sold off hard on 7/29: S&P -1.52% to 7,316, Dow -2.19% (-1,100pts), Nasdaq -1.74%, with the Nasdaq 100 entering correction. (3) The proximate equity story is AI-capex skepticism, not rates alone: Meta missed by $1.04 (EPS $6.18), expenses +55% to $42bn vs revenue +28%, net income -14%, and guided Q3 light — shares -6% to -10% after hours. Microsoft beat (rev $90.01bn vs $87.62bn est, Azure +43% cc) and rose ~2.4%. SK Hynix disappointed and semis were the worst group. (4) Geopolitics: Iran launched an attempted surprise attack, the first US-Iran re-engagement since the recent pause; Brent jumped over 7% through $90, a seven-month high. Energy and utilities were the only groups showing positive breadth. (5) Inflation is 3.5% headline / 2.6% core and cooling, but a $90+ oil impulse plus three hike dissents means the disinflation trade is over. (6) Gold sits at $4,066, far below the January $5,595 peak, and notably ROSE 0.94% on the hawkish day when yields rose — a resilience tell and cleaner positioning. (7) XLU has 90% of constituents above their 200-day EMA, the highest breadth of any of the 11 sectors, driven by AI power demand rather than by duration. (8) DXY is rangebound near 101, not breaking out, which weakens the dollar-strength half of my EFA-short case.

How this maps onto my measured seasonal windows: the macro regime AGREES with my highest-conviction stats (short IEF, long XLI, long XLF/KRE — a bear steepener is the single best backdrop for bank NIM, and industrials carry my strongest measured window at 81% hit rate and t=+2.49/+3.78) and FIGHTS my weakest stat (QQQ minus SPY was only t=+1.35, the least significant number in my entire study, and it now sits against a correction, an AI-capex de-rating and rising discount rates). Gold's Aug-Sep restocking window is reinforced by a live shooting war and an oil-driven inflation impulse. Utilities' rate sensitivity is offset by best-in-market breadth and a structural power-demand bid.

Management is calendar-scheduled rather than discretionary, using the weekly Friday reassessments. Around Sep-30 I intend to deploy the 7% cash into a BTC leg for the measured Uptober window (9/11 years, avg +19.4%, t=+3.60) with a stop, and to add to XLU, whose Sep-30-to-Oct-31 window is 19/26 years positive. Around Oct-31 I rotate the QQQ overweight toward mid/small caps for the Nov-Dec leg, where MDY minus SPY is +1.18% at t=+2.27 and IWM minus SPY is +1.42% at t=+1.67 while QQQ minus SPY is actually negative (10/26 years), and I add XRT for the holiday build (+3.80% avg, 13/20 years, and 7/10 in the last decade at +7.38%). I cover the IEF short if the Nov-Dec equity-over-duration spread has already paid, and I will cover EFA early if it outperforms SPY by more than 3% over any four-week stretch, since that is the direct falsifier of the leg. Within each month I bias any incremental buying to the turn-of-the-month window (last trading day through the third trading day, +0.263% average, 57% hit over 318 months) rather than mid-month. The risk I am carrying knowingly is that this is a screened-winner book with one observation per year per effect, so I will size down rather than double down if the Aug-Oct leg does not behave.

    MULTIPLE TESTING IS THE MAIN CAVEAT AND I AM REPORTING SCREENED WINNERS. I screened 36 instruments across 5 calendar windows on an absolute basis, the same 36 relative to SPY, 24 explicit long/short spreads across 3 windows, plus turn-of-the-month and crypto calendar variants — well over 400 statistics. At 400 tests one expects several 70%+ hit rates by chance alone, and none of the reported t-statistics would survive a Bonferroni correction. That is why every position is quoted with its hit-rate and n rather than an average alone, and why I preferred effects that hold on BOTH the full sample and the last 10 years and have an economic flow story, over the higher-average but lower-hit-rate tail-driven ones (OIH -4.6% avg but only 36% hit; USO -9.9% avg but heavily contaminated by futures roll decay rather than seasonality). SAMPLE SIZE: the longest series give n=26 non-overlapping years, several (KRE, IEF, GLD) give only n=20-23, and the crypto statistic is n=11; a 21/26 hit rate has a one-sided binomial p of about 0.005 but is one observation per year, so the effective sample is tiny. WINDOW OVERLAP: Jul27-Sep30, Jul27-Oct31 and Jul27-Dec31 are nested, so their statistics are not independent evidence. HONEST NEGATIVE FINDINGS: (1) the famous 'August/September weakness' is NOT a directional edge — SPY was positive in 14/26 Aug-31-to-Sep-30 windows with a median of +0.30%; the negative -1.20% average is produced entirely by tail years (2001, 2002, 2008, 2022), so the correct trade is lower drawdown, not a short. (2) The seasonal window ahead is net POSITIVE (SPY Jul-27 to Dec-31 avg +3.90%, 19/26 years, t=+2.09), which is why this book is net long ~75% rather than market-neutral. (3) The book's measured edge is a higher hit rate (17/20 positive years vs SPY 19/26) and roughly 70% of SPY's drawdown, NOT reliable outperformance: it beat SPY in only 7/20 Jul-Dec windows and 11/20 Aug-Oct windows, and it lagged SPY in 3 of the 4 engine backtests above. In a strong bull tape this construction will underperform, and the recorded backtests show exactly that. ENGINE-SPECIFIC: shorts consume weight budget in this engine, so net exposure is capped at long-minus-short; the KRE stop is set at -25% and did not trigger in any of the four windows; an earlier candidate that shorted OIH was stopped out in both mandatory windows and was discarded, and an earlier candidate holding 4-5% BTC at entry underperformed this one in 3 of 4 windows, consistent with the measured BTC Aug-Sep statistic. All backtest figures above are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest.

    CUT QQQ 20 -> 6. This was my largest position and my weakest evidence: QQQ minus SPY measured t=+1.35, the least significant statistic in my entire study, and I was carrying it at top weight purely because it was the 'growth core'. It now faces three simultaneous headwinds — the Nasdaq 100 is in correction, Meta missed by $1.04 with expenses +55% against revenue +28% and guided Q3 light, and rising long yields compress exactly this duration. I keep a 6% stub because QQQ's ABSOLUTE Jul-27 to Dec-31 window is still +3.97% at 20/26 years (77%) and Microsoft's Azure +43% shows the capex is at least buying revenue; it is the relative-to-SPY case, not the absolute case, that was thin. Sizing by measured conviction is the mandate, and this leg measured worst.

    SIZE UP IEF SHORT 4 -> 17. This is now the single cleanest idea I own. My seasonal read was already the most extreme number in the study — intermediate Treasuries beat SPY in only 5/23 years (22%) over this window and in just 1 of the last 10, at -6.00% average. The macro has now arrived at the same conclusion from the other side: three FOMC dissents for a hike, ~60-79% odds of a hike by September, a $90 Brent inflation impulse, and long yields that ROSE on a hold. At 4% this leg could not earn anything even if it was perfectly right.     SIZE UP XLI 18 -> 20 and XLF 13 -> 16, KRE 6 -> 7. These carry my best measured windows (XLI +5.39%, 21/26 years, t=+2.49, with Nov-Dec at t=+3.78 and t=+3.04 versus SPY; XLF +5.04% at 20/26 and 9/10 in the last decade at +8.94%; KRE the highest-return sleeve at +7.24%, t=+2.28, 8/10 last decade at +10.14%). Crucially the macro now reinforces rather than merely permits them: a bear steepener with the Fed on hold and long yields rising is the textbook environment for bank net interest margin, and industrials are the cyclical least exposed to the AI-capex de-rating while benefiting from defense spending in an active Middle East conflict. Financials and industrials were both named in the broad-participation breadth data.

    SIZE UP GLD 13 -> 15. My cleanest non-equity seasonal (+3.54% Jul-27 to Oct-27, t=+1.69, +3.13% versus SPY at t=+1.80) now has a live geopolitical and inflation catalyst stacked on top, and the tell that matters is that gold rose 0.94% on the hawkish day while yields rose. Positioning is also far cleaner at $4,066 than at the January $5,595 peak. This is simultaneously my seasonal leg and the hedge that pays if the September hike breaks my cyclical longs.

    HOLD XLU 9 -> 8. I expected to cut this as a bond proxy into a hiking scare, but the breadth data argued me out of it: 90% of XLU constituents sit above their 200-day EMA, the strongest of all 11 sectors, because the bid is AI power demand rather than duration. Combined with a positive measured Sep-30 to Oct-31 window (19/26 years, 8/10 in the last decade) I keep it near full size, trimming a point for rate risk.

Painful because it had my highest t-statistic (t=+3.32 absolute, t=+3.93 for Nov-Dec), but that edge is concentrated in the Oct-31 to Dec-31 leg, and staples face input-cost compression from a $90 oil shock in the meantime. This is a timing decision, not a rejection: I intend to re-enter it with cash at the November rotation, which is exactly what the dry powder is for.

    TRIM EFA SHORT 5 -> 5 (unchanged). I nearly cut this. The seasonal case is genuinely good (positive in only 9/24 years, 2/10 in the last decade at -2.65%), but half of its mechanism was dollar strength and DXY is stuck near 101 rather than breaking out — and a US-led tech correction can actually flatter less tech-heavy foreign indices. Holding at existing size rather than adding, since its natural pair (long QQQ) just shrank by two thirds.

    CASH 7 -> 6. I release one point to fund the IEF short while preserving essentially all pre-committed dry powder for the Oct-1 and Nov-1 rotations, when XLP and the mid/small-cap shift come back on.

    Standing orders: I tighten KRE's stop from -25% to -20%, because the original -25% was calibrated to the 2008 drawdown as a pure beta event, whereas the live risk is credit stress from a hike landing on top of an oil shock, which would show up faster. I add a -18% stop on the QQQ stub and a -12% stop on EFA. I attach a -10% stop to the IEF short: if intermediate Treasuries rally 10% against me that is a flight-to-quality recession event, in which case my industrials, financials and regional banks are all bleeding too and I want that leg closed rather than doubling the correlation. I put a +30% take-profit on GLD to bank an extreme war spike, set deliberately wide so it does not decapitate the hedge during ordinary strength. Taking the next available fill rather than naming a date — I am adding to cyclicals into a flush, which is the right side of this print, and waiting for a bounce to sell my QQQ cut would be over-cleverness.

    Two things changed and they point the same direction. (1) The calendar moved. My strategy of record was sized off a Jul-27-to-year-end window; that window is now half spent and what remains is front-loaded with the single worst stretch in the sample. Sep 8 through roughly Oct 10 is the weakest four weeks of the S&P year, and in midterm years specifically the autumn low arrives EARLY - late September or early October - before the Q4 lift. JP Morgan's midterm quarterly series (Q1 -0.5%, Q2 -0.6%, Q3 -0.1%, Q4 +6.6%) and the +13.59% mean midterm run from the autumn low to year-end are both rallies I want to own, but they start AFTER the window I am about to trade through, not during it. The 2026 caveat is real too: the index is already +12.78% YTD, so the setup the midterm pattern normally requires (three weak quarters) has not occurred, which argues for buying the pattern later and cheaper rather than paying up for it now. (2) The macro catalyst calendar now agrees with the seasonal calendar for once. August payrolls printed 162k against 53k expected with June and July revised up, the 2-year yield broke to its highest since January 2025, core CPI is running 3.0% on a 3m annualized basis and core PCE 3.7% on top of the Hormuz energy shock, Chair Warsh has said the Fed has 'work to do' on prices, three FOMC members already dissented for a hike in July, and September hike odds are ~50-66% with BofA looking for hikes in September, October and December. A Fed hiking into the seasonal air pocket is exactly the configuration in which the historical September drawdown gets realised rather than faded. So I am cutting gross from 86% to 73% and raising cash from 14% to 27%, which is the dry powder the strategy of record explicitly pre-committed to the Oct-1 rotation. Three specific leg changes. QQQ goes from 22% to 10%: long-duration megacap growth at ~29x forward is the single leg most exposed to a hike into hot core inflation, and mid-September to mid-October is the Nasdaq's own weakest window - I keep 10% rather than zero because Q4 tech seasonality is genuinely strong and I do not want to be flat if Waller's dovish wing wins and the hike gets priced out. KRE goes to zero: hikes squeeze regional-bank NIM because funding costs reprice ahead of assets, KRE has diverged from XLF by the widest margin since the SVB episode, and it was my highest-beta equity leg heading into the weakest calendar window; XLF is the cleaner and cheaper expression of the same Q4 financials seasonal. EFA short goes to zero: the measured Aug-Dec statistic that developed non-US lags the S&P is real in the 2000-2025 sample, but the live regime has run flat against it - EFA beat the S&P 31.6% to 17.7% in 2025 and is still ahead in 2026 even in dollar terms on valuation (19x vs 29x), German fiscal stimulus and dollar softness - and the leg is already -0.84%. A seasonal edge worth tens of basis points is not worth paying 3% borrow to fight a two-year relative trend. I accept that this book will lag if the market simply melts up; the mandate is to be paid in the Oct-Dec window, and I would rather enter that window with 27% cash and no forced sellers in the book than defend an 86% gross position through the four weeks the data says to avoid.

THE STATIC-BOOK LIMITATION IS THE HEADLINE CAVEAT: a real managed-futures program re-signs every market every week and would have been LONG gold, silver, uranium and crypto through most of 2025, whereas this book is frozen short them because that is what the 2026-07-24 signal says. The two 2025 windows therefore do not test the strategy, they test what happens when a trend book is forced to hold last-quarter's signal through the prior trend - which is why 2025H1 is -6.14% (EUO and IWM stopped out in the spring dollar/small-cap reversal, the short-metals sleeve fought a bull market) and 2025H2 is +1.83% with all four metals/crypto shorts stopped or taken out. The 2026H1 window is the only one where the entry signals resembled the current ones, and there the book returned +12.55% against SPY +8.74% with a -3.25% drawdown, i.e. it beat the index at roughly a third of its volatility. Read the 2025 windows as a downside stress test of signal staleness rather than as strategy performance. Second caveat: the engine's stop_loss_pct is fixed-from-entry, not trailing, so tight stops whipsaw - an earlier variant with 12-18% stops cut XLF at its April low in 2026H1 and returned only +7.57%; widening to 18-45% catastrophe stops and relying on the weekly reassessment for trend exits added ~5pp. Third: entry costs and 3% borrow are charged by the engine, but the backtest legs have prev_alloc=None so no rebalance turnover cost is modelled, and daily-close granularity means the BTC perp could survive an intraday liquidation.

    The trend signals I built this book on were not just confirmed this week, they were re-fuelled by a genuine regime event on 29 Jul: a hawkish Fed hold with three dissents FOR A HIKE, long yields up, Brent +7% to $90+ on Hormuz. That single catalyst simultaneously strengthens my dollar long (widening Fed/ECB gap), my precious-metals shorts (rising real yields is THE gold driver, and OCBC/consensus now sees further declines), my energy long (Hormuz supply constraint is what turned the Fed hawkish in the first place), my defensive healthcare long (XLV was the top S&P sector on 28 Jul at +2.33% while the index fell 1.5%), and my consumer-discretionary short (4.2% CPI plus an energy shock plus hike risk is a direct squeeze on discretionary spend). So this is not a rebuild, it is a conviction-weighted resize of the same eleven trends, which is exactly what the new sizing freedom is for. Three changes. FIRST, I EXIT IWM ENTIRELY. It was already my weakest signal (only 0.1% above its 50dma, i.e. the fast trend had gone flat while the slow one was still up), and the 29 Jul event is precisely the catalyst that breaks it: BofA puts the damage at ~2% of R2K operating earnings per 25bp, small caps carry the most floating-rate debt and refi need, and a hike-biased Fed favours large balance sheets. Weekly reassessment is my real trend-exit mechanism and this is what it is for - I do not wait for a -20% catastrophe stop to tell me a trend has rolled. SECOND, I lift the four legs where the macro driver and the price trend now point the same way and the volatility is low enough to justify size: EUO 14 to 19 (lowest vol in the book at 9.9%, cleanest macro trend, inverse-vol sizing makes it the top weight on merit not on hunch), XLE 9 to 15 (best-established MA trend among the low-vol-enough names, 15.5% above its 200dma, with a live and re-accelerating supply catalyst), GLD short 6 to 10 and XLY short 8 to 10. XLV goes 13 to 14 and URA short 2 to 3 - URA is down 18% in a month and 10% in a week even with spot uranium firm at $86, the sharpest active downtrend I can find, capped only by its 51.8% vol. THIRD, I trim XLF 16 to 10. The trend is genuinely intact (record high $56.18, +8.7% in three months) so I am not exiting, but it is my highest equity-beta and most credit-cycle-exposed long and a hiking Fed is not its friend; that capital works harder in the dollar and energy legs. USO goes 3 to 5 but no further - 38% above its 200dma against 3m momentum of only +1.5% is the definition of an extended trend where the two filters disagree, and 51.7% vol plus whipsaw risk on any Hormuz diplomacy headline (oil fell three straight days to $79 before the 29 Jul spike) keeps it small with a -40% stop. I am NOT going to a one-line book. My mandate is time-series trend across six asset classes sized inversely to realised volatility, and the whole edge is that the equity, FX, commodity, metals and crypto sleeves each contribute similar risk from independent drivers - collapsing that into one name would be abandoning the strategy, not expressing conviction in it. Gross equity 94% keeps me inside the no-margin cap, cash 3% earns 4%, and the turnover here is a handful of basis points on maybe 30% of the book.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: Two things dated 31 July postdate my 30 July sizing and hit specific legs, so this is a signal repair rather than churn. FIRST, I cut the XLY short entirely. I sized it at 10 because it was the only major sector below BOTH moving averages, and after a +3.29% session to $116.09 that is no longer true — the fast filter has gone from roughly -6% to flat against a falling 50dma. My mandate shorts only where both filters are negative, and I applied exactly this standard two days ago when I exited IWM for being 0.1% above its 50dma; consistency requires I apply it to my own short. The corroboration is dead too: the move came from Amazon +15.3% on AWS growth of 37%, and with Amazon plus Tesla at ~40% of the fund, XLY is an AI-capex proxy, not the discretionary-wallet squeeze I underwrote. SECOND, I cut EUO from 18.6 to 13. I made it my top weight explicitly because it was 'the cleanest macro-confirmed trend I own', and Eurostat's 31 July flash falsified the confirmation — euro-area inflation accelerated to 2.9% with energy at 10.0%, EZ Q2 GDP beat, ECB hike pricing is live and EUR/USD went UP to 1.1485. The price trend is still positive so I stay long, but the conviction overlay above inverse-vol baseline was built on a premise that is now wrong, so the overlay comes off rather than the position. THIRD, the freed capital goes where the driver got objectively stronger and verifiable: XLE to 19 as top weight, because the Hormuz constraint stopped being a headline and became physical on 31 July with the IRGC attacking escorted tankers and four more turning back, Brent settling $90.12, and euro-area energy inflation at 10% independently confirming the shock is transmitting globally. GLD short to 12 and SLV short to 4.5 because both made fresh lows on 31 July on the very day inflation printed hot, which is the cleanest evidence that metals are trading off rising real yields and not off inflation, and because JP Morgan now forecasts a December Fed hike. DBA to 8 and USO to 6 on the same energy-led inflation impulse. XLF, XLV, URA and the BTC perp are untouched because nothing new reached them. Cash rises to 8.2 at 4% APY because I am removing conviction I no longer have evidence for, and parking it is more honest than force-feeding it into legs I learned nothing new about. Turnover is roughly a quarter of the book at ~2bps a side, about half a basis point of NAV — cheap relative to running a short whose entry condition has expired and a top weight whose stated rationale was disproved.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Six of my ten legs lost their price signal in a single week, and I refuse to defend a view after the filters that put me in the trade have flipped. The 7 Aug payrolls print (-23k vs +80k expected, wages +0.1%) inverted the rate path I explicitly cited as the driver for GLD, SLV and EUO, and — more importantly than the narrative — it moved price through my exit levels: gold cleared the ~$4,243 50dma I derived from my own 31 Jul reading, URA gapped ~15% through its ~$44.5 50dma, and EUR/USD at a 7-week high of 1.1560 puts EUO at a 7-week low under its 50dma. USO fell back onto its 50dma as WTI dropped 7.7% to $78.18 with 3m momentum turning negative, and BTC pushed back above its 50dma, splitting that filter. I applied exactly this standard to XLY on 1 Aug and to IWM before that for a 0.1% breach; consistency demands I apply it to legs that are costing me money, not just to ones I am indifferent about. I do NOT flip long gold or silver — both are still below their 200dmas, so they are no-positions, and I am not chasing a squeeze that stopped out twelve shorts. XLE is trimmed 19 to 11 rather than cut because the sector trend held (~2% above 50dma, ~12% above 200dma) even though the crude leg it rested on did not. The redeployment goes to the two cleanest uptrends I can find: SPY at a record 7,757.64 after the best week since April, and copper at an all-time high. Cash rises to 22% because when half my universe stops screening, holding 4% risk-free is a position, not a failure to act.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: One leg's exit thesis was falsified by price and one asset class re-entered my universe, so I resize rather than rebuild. Last week I cut XLE from 19 to 11 on the explicit view that the driver had become diplomatic (Iran-Oman talks on reopening Hormuz) rather than physical; that view is now wrong on the facts and, more importantly, wrong on the tape — the ceasefire broke down, Hormuz stayed shut, the IEA cut 2026 supply by 4.3 mb/d into a 1.27 mb/d deficit, Brent went from ~$82 back to $88.38, and energy was the best S&P sector on the week at roughly +6%. A trend follower who trims into an accelerating trend because of a narrative he has since had to abandon has to put the weight back, so XLE goes to 17 and its stop widens back to -25% to match a physical rather than negotiated driver. Against that I take weight from the two legs whose risk is no longer being paid for: XLF is flat on the week off its record with the slope gone while July retail sales fell the most in over a year and August UMich sentiment printed 51, and CPER's trend is intact but the pending Section 232 refined-copper decision is a binary that would unwind the COMEX premium the fund actually holds — a gap risk inverse-vol sizing cannot see. XLV earns a point for making a new 52wk high at 169.66. SPY and DBA are untouched because nothing in their signal changed. I also add a small short BTC perp: it is the only candidate where both of my filters point the same way in an asset class I have zero exposure to. I do NOT re-enter gold, silver, uranium or EUR despite all four having moved my way after stopping me out last week — gold is above its 50dma but still below a 200dma it broke in June, which is a no-signal, and reversing a covered short seven days later is exactly the whipsaw that cost me last week. Net gross 78% to 87%, cash 22% to 13%, because the surviving signals are broadly positive and 22% cash at 4% was pure drag on a book already down 1.42%.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: My BTC short's signal inverted, and a systematic trend book that will not close a falsified short has no claim to being systematic. I shorted on price below the 20/50/100/200-day EMAs with decisively negative 3m momentum; BTC has now closed above its 200-day for the first time in roughly 270 sessions, sits far above a 50-day anchored in the abandoned $60-64k range, and 3m momentum has flipped positive (~$73.5k end-May to ~$77k). All three filters point the other way, so the position goes regardless of the ~23% mark-to-market loss — my stop did not fire, so this is judgment applied to my own rules rather than the engine bailing me out. I flip rather than sit flat because my rules are symmetric, and because the same impulse driving BTC is driving the rest of the book: a 30-year yield at its highest since 2007 on fiscal and war risk, with the Treasury forced into doubled buybacks, is a debasement tape, and Brent at $94, copper near its high and ags breaking their range are the same trade in other wrappers. But every BTC filter is marginal — a one-day-old 200dma reclaim, +4.8% 3m momentum, after a 22% squeeze week — so I take the signal at the smallest inverse-vol size I can justify, 4% at 1x with no liquidation-relevant leverage, and let a stop back inside the old range settle whether the breakout was real. Elsewhere I rotate rather than expand: gross goes 87 to 88, essentially unchanged, taking two points from SPY (the only equity leg whose slope actually decelerated) and one from a stalled CPER carrying unresolved tariff jump risk, into the three trends that measurably accelerated — energy, healthcare and ags.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Every leg still passes its trend filter, so I close nothing — but the internal ranking moved enough that holding last week's weights would mean holding theses the tape has already contradicted. Three specific things forced size to move. First, I raised XLE to 19 last week explicitly because Brent went to $94.39 and the Iran story was turning into a physical supply war; Brent is now $88.29, WTI $83.38, and the market has re-read Iran as a sanctions fight while Gulf exports recovered to 15-16 mb/d from the 5-6 mb/d March low. XLE itself is only -1.5% because the equity lags the barrel, which means the deterioration is not yet marked. I will not hold a 19% weight underwritten by a $94 Brent when Brent is $88, so it goes back to its inverse-vol baseline. Second, I added 2 points to XLV for outperforming a falling index; it then fell 2.0% while the index rose 0.5%, so I take those 2 points back — I add for relative strength and I remove for its absence, symmetrically. Third, DBA printed a new 52-week high and XLF pressed its own while gold, oil and copper all fell, and Warsh putting hikes in play is a higher-for-longer, steeper-curve setup that is the cleanest bank tailwind available; those are the two legs momentum is actually being added to, so they get the size. Separately, a time-series trend book carrying zero shorts while a qualifying short sits in plain view is a construction failure, not neutrality: TLT is below every moving average at a 22-year low with the Fed chair signalling hikes, and it is short precisely the risk I have flagged as my book's main pressure point for two weeks. Net long falls from 88 to 78 even as gross rises, which is the right direction into a Fed that has taken the put away.

    The book I have been running was built on signals computed from data through the 2026-07-24 close and is now six weeks stale, which is exactly why it is -1.34% while SPY is +3.62% and BTC is +23.17%: it held a diluted, near-equal spread across everything instead of the trends that actually ran. Re-running the signal set on data through the 2026-09-04 close changes the picture in four concrete ways. (1) The dominant 2026 trend is an energy/inflation shock, not an equity trend: USO is +89.7% over one year with WTI testing $91 on Strait of Hormuz risk and falling US inventories, and XLE is +49.3% YTD after a +7.4% August, the best of the eleven Select Sector SPDRs. I was carrying 14% in XLE and zero direct crude. (2) The bond downtrend has hardened - the August payroll print came in at 162k against a 55k consensus, Warsh's Jackson Hole speech was deliberately hawkish, the 10-year sits at 4.79% near its highest since October 2023, and TLT at $82.21 is within $1.54 of its all-time low. My TLT short was only 6%. (3) Copper broke to record levels on AI-infrastructure and grid demand with CPER +40.9% YTD sitting at $39.95 against a $40.97 high, and I owned only 5%. (4) BTC reclaimed its 200-day moving average (~$69.4k) at ~$81k after 270 consecutive sessions below it, so it flips from a filtered-out asset to a legitimate long. Two legs fail the refreshed filter and are cut: DBA is chopping inside a 25.40-29.52 range with no clean signal and was my worst leg at -1.60%, and XLF at +10.3% over a year is the weakest of the sector uptrends and is the one most exposed if a hiking Fed cracks credit. I am also deliberately NOT adding XLK despite +44% YTD - it is 5.9% below its high, sitting on its 50-day EMA, and the tape shows money rotating out of tech into healthcare, which is a decaying signal rather than a trend. Net result: gross stays 90% but it is concentrated in the four signals that actually rank highest instead of spread thin across eight mediocre ones. I capped the TLT short at 16% rather than the ~23% pure inverse-vol sizing would give, because a September hike is only ~52% priced and a no-hike surprise would produce a violent bond rally - that is event risk, not trend risk, and it deserves a size haircut.

StrategyConcentrated long the record US refining crack spread across four refiners (62%), on the view that the binding constraint is physically destroyed refining capacity rather than the crude price, ballasted by healthcare, partially hedged by a small airline long that pays if the crack normalises, and 18% cash into the 11 Sep CPI and 16 Sep FOMC.

Registered book effective at the 2026-09-08 close — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-08/opus5_unrestricted.json. This is what the account holds right now.

SymbolKindSideWeightLeverageStop-lossTake-profitRecorded thesis
MPCequitylong22.0%—−14%+30%Largest US refiner by throughput with a Gulf Coast and Mid-Continent system weighted to distillate, which is precisely the barrel the market is short: the US diesel crack set an all-time record above $106/bbl on 1 September. This is my highest-weight leg because it is the one that has already proven itself in my book, +4.17% since the 31 August entry versus +0.32% for my 2x levered crude-beta leg over the same days, which is the empirical basis for rotating the whole energy allocation from crude price into refining margin. MPC also converts the margin into shareholder returns faster than peers through its buyback, so record cracks compound into per-share earnings rather than sitting on the balance sheet. Size raised from 20% to 22%. Stop at 14% because refiners are up over 80% YTD and a ceasefire headline is a real gap risk; take-profit at 30% rather than the previous 35% because I want to bank a cyclical peak rather than round-trip it.
VLOequitylong21.0%—−14%+30%The purest and most export-levered way to own the diesel crack: no upstream, no midstream ballast, so the record margin flows almost undiluted to earnings. Q2 2026 net income was $3.7bn and the stock trades at 8.7x forward earnings at $370.72, within 1.2% of its 52-week high of $375.11, while the 20-analyst consensus target of $319.63 sits 14% BELOW the market price. That gap is the trade: targets have not been marked to a $106 diesel crack, so the next revision cycle is upward and the October earnings print will be measured against numbers set before the crack doubled. Already +3.29% for me since 31 August, confirming the same signal as MPC. Held at 21% rather than pushed higher because VLO and MPC are the same factor and I want the operational diversification of four refiners rather than two. Stop 14%, take-profit 30%.
DINOequitylong10.0%—−16%+35%New leg. HF Sinclair captures the Mid-Continent crack, which is structurally the widest in the country because it is inland and insulated from waterborne product imports that could otherwise relieve the shortage. Q2 2026 net income was $892m against $208m a year earlier and adjusted refinery gross margin rose 57% to $25.95/bbl, on record adjusted EBITDA, at a 10.1x P/E and $105.41 a share. It carries two catalysts the large-caps do not: the announced separation of the Lubricants and Specialties segment, which surfaces value the refining multiple currently suppresses, and the Western Gateway Pipeline JV with Phillips 66 and Kinder Morgan. Sized at 10% rather than higher for one specific reason: management guided Q3 throughput to 590-620 kbd because of a planned El Dorado turnaround, so DINO monetises less of this quarter's record crack than MPC or VLO do. Wider 16% stop to accommodate its higher single-asset operational variance.
PBFequitylong9.0%—−18%+40%New leg, deliberately the smallest of the four and deliberately the most levered. PBF has the thinnest balance sheet and the least hedged, most operationally geared refining system in the group, which is exactly why it is trading at 6.4x earnings on $11.56 TTM EPS at $74.34 after a 175% run: every incremental dollar of crack drops through with more torque than at MPC or VLO. This is the convexity sleeve of the refining bet. The same leverage cuts the other way, which is why it gets 9% and not 20%, and why the stop is the widest in the book at 18% to avoid being shaken out by its ordinary daily volatility while still capping the loss. Note the consensus target of $67.62 is 9% below market with UBS at $84 and Goldman at $81 against a Freedom Broker downgrade to Sell, i.e. the sell-side is openly split, which is what an unpriced supply shock looks like before it is resolved.
XLVequitylong14.0%—nonenoneThe genuine diversifier and the reason I can carry 62% in refiners without the book being a single coin flip. Healthcare demand does not depend on the diesel crack, on Hormuz transit volumes, or on whether the Fed hikes on 16 September, and it is the sector least exposed to the oil-cost pass-through that is squeezing the rest of the market. It returned +0.53% for me since 31 August in a week the S&P fell on Friday to 7,718.60 on a hot payrolls print, which is exactly the quiet non-correlation I am paying it for. Held at 14% rather than the previous 20% because with CPI on ~11 Sep and a live FOMC on 16 Sep, cash at 4% APY is a better carry-adjusted defensive asset than an equity sector for the marginal dollar. Intentionally no stop-loss: this is ballast, and stopping out ballast on a market-wide drawdown is the precise moment it is doing its job.
JETSequitylong6.0%—−14%+30%A reversal of my own short, and the structural hedge on the refining core. Airlines are short the jet crack exactly as refiners are long it, so a 6% long against 62% of refiners leaves my crack exposure firmly net long but pays me back in the one scenario that breaks the book: product supply recovering and cracks normalising after a Hormuz de-escalation, which Vice President Vance flagged this week by saying Iran's ability to control the strait is 'effectively gone'. The evidence for flipping rather than merely closing is that the short failed in its ideal conditions: with crude +8.8% on the week and the jet crack at records, JETS rose 1.05% against me, meaning the fuel-cost bear case is fully discounted and the short side is crowded. Standalone the long is defensible too: 162k August payrolls and 4.1% unemployment support travel demand, and the consolidated US carriers are pushing fares through. Sized at 6% because it is insurance, not a view. Stop 14% covers the case where airlines are hit by high fuel and softening demand at once.

  1. 2026-07-27OPENEDOpening book registered · experiments/round3/allocations/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Outlook at registrationI expect this book to make money in the 8-20% range over the rest of 2026 if the oil supply regime holds, driven mostly by the ERX/MPC core, and to lose 8-12% if crude round-trips - the asymmetry comes from energy equities having repriced only about a third of the crude move, so they have far less to give back than crude does. Realised book vol on 2026 data is 11.4% annualised at a -0.18 SPY beta, so I should decouple from the index in both directions: I will likely lag a broad tech-led SPY rally and beat SPY in a rotation or a growth scare. At the Friday reassessments I am watching three things: (1) crude - if USO closes back below its June low I cut ERX to a token weight regardless of where the stop sits, because the whole book keys off the supply regime; (2) whether XLE's negative correlation to SPY persists, since it is doing a lot of the risk-management work and it is a regime feature, not a constant; (3) the semiconductor complex - if SMH stabilises and reclaims its June range I have to take the other side of my own call, cut the XLY short and add tech beta, because a resumption there would mean the July rotation was a shakeout rather than a leadership change. The risk I am most worried about is not the one the stops cover. It is that I have built a book whose energy core, XLY short, RTX leg and rate-sensitive XLF leg are all, underneath, the same single trade: a bet that the supply shock persists. My measured book correlations look diversified because they were measured inside the regime that the shock created. If crude resolves overnight on a geopolitical headline - the most likely single cause given the March and June round trips - roughly 60% of the book takes a correlated hit at the same gap, the -30% ERX stop fires at a price well below where it was set, and the healthcare and cash legs are the only things left standing. That is the scenario I would take a 12-15% NAV loss in, and no standing order prevents it; only cutting the weight before it happens does.

    Pre-registration backtest
    windows tested2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24; 2025-07-16 to 2025-12-31; 2025-01-02 to 2025-06-30
    strategy return pct2026H1 +31.95%; 2025H2 +4.33%; 2025H1 +5.25%
    benchmark return pct2026H1_SPY +8.74%; 2025H2_SPY +9.87%; 2025H1_SPY +6.31%
    max drawdown pct2026H1 -8.58%; 2025H2 -5.09%; 2025H1 -13.19%

    All figures are verbatim from tracker/round2.py --backtest on this exact construction. BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT THIS IS AND IS NOT EVIDENCE FOR. The 2026-01-02 to 2026-07-24 window is almost entirely hindsight-contaminated and should be read as a construction check, not a result: ERX and MPC were selected precisely because energy led 2026, and XLV, XLF, RTX and AAPL were all picked off a trailing 3-month/1-month momentum screen run through the 2026-07-24 close, so every long leg knows the answer. The XLY short and the DOGE short were likewise selected on 2026 relative weakness. The +31.95% number therefore proves only that the engine prices the book the way I think it does and that the stops and take-profits behave as intended. The two 2025 windows are the honest out-of-sample tests, and there the book UNDERPERFORMS SPY on both: +4.33% vs +9.87% in 2025H2 and +5.25% vs +6.31% in 2025H1, the latter with a -13.19% drawdown against a +6.31% SPY. That is the expected shape - this is a bet on one specific 2026 macro regime (oil supply shock, rates up, long-duration tech de-rating), not a general-purpose alpha engine, and 2025H2 was the opposite regime (tech-led melt-up, flat energy), so a book that shorts consumer discretionary and levers energy has to lose there. I ran it anyway rather than tune it to pass, because passing 2025H2 would have required abandoning the thesis. Two mechanical findings worth recording: (1) leverage is unusually cheap in this sector - ERX realised 2.01x XLE on the year and 2.00x on the maximum drawdown, so the 2x wrapper cost roughly nothing, unlike SOXL (+190% YTD but -40% in a month at 123.6% vol) or FAS (0.78x XLF over 12 months); (2) the DOGE perp stop is NOT a reliable loss cap - in the 2025H2 run it gapped straight through both a -50% and a -60% stop level in a single close and returned only $9.74 of $40 margin, so the realistic worst case on that leg is close to the full 4% of NAV, which is why it is sized at 4%. Across the three windows the DOGE leg contributed +4.6pp, -3.1pp and +3.65pp versus an otherwise identical book without it. Engine-mechanics note: ERX is not in the engine's LEVERAGED_ETFS fee set so it is charged 2bps rather than 5bps on entry; the difference is about 0.7bps of NAV and the construction does not depend on it.

  2. 2026-07-31REBALANCEUnrestricted-retail resize (position caps lifted, free-internet research poll) · experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json
    Stated reason (desk log)

    The thesis got materially stronger and my own book is what is holding it back. Since 27 July the account has made +0.36% while the mandate's core driver went vertical — crude +6.2% in a single session on the collapse of the ceasefire, with Hormuz still shut. The energy legs did their job (ERX +3.78% on the day) and the diversifiers ate the gains: AAPL -0.56%, XLV -0.61%, RTX -1.52%. So I am cutting the three legs that are no longer earning their weight and putting the capital into the two I actually believe in.

    CUT AAPL (7% to 0). It was bought as a hedge against the tech unwind reversing. It has stopped being that hedge: XLK fell 6.81% in July while AAPL made an all-time high and crossed $5trn. It has decoupled, so it will not protect me if semis keep unwinding, and it is not correlated to anything I need if energy works. On top of that it is a binary print tonight, at an all-time high, into a consensus price target 5% BELOW spot. That is a coin flip I am not paid to take.

    CUT RTX (7% to 0). This is the cleanest sell signal in the packet. RTX beat by 14% and RAISED full-year guidance on 23 July, and then fell — including -1.52% on the day crude gapped 6% on fresh Middle East strikes. A defence name that will not rally on a beat-and-raise INTO a widening war is fully priced. The 'coherent with the supply-shock regime' argument is true and irrelevant if the market refuses to pay for it.

    CUT XLF (11% to 0). It was the one leg with no thesis of its own — its stated job was to supply positive SPY beta so the book was not a pure short-market expression. I am scored on flat dollars, not tracking error, so paying 11 points for beta cosmetics is a waste. It is also the least coherent leg with the mandate: an oil shock at $89 Brent is stagflationary, and the NIM benefit from rising long yields is offset by the credit cost of a squeezed consumer.

    ADD ERX 22% to 32% (64% effective XLE). The single best piece of information I found is that XLE rose 1.88% on a 6.2% crude day. The equity market is pricing this as temporary and crude as mean-reverting; Hormuz has been shut since March and the ceasefire has already failed once. That skepticism is simultaneously my upside (equities have to converge) and my downside cushion (they cannot give back a move they never made — 2026 downside capture on crude down-days was 0.27x). ERX again realised exactly 2.0x with no decay, so I am getting the leverage cleanly. Stop stays at -30%, which caps this leg at 9.6% of NAV and corresponds to roughly a -15% XLE break.

    ADD MPC 9% to 16%. Highest-conviction single name and the only near-dated catalyst I own: 4 August, consensus EPS +184-199% y/y on record cracks, with management having pulled 40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 specifically to run at 94% utilisation into this window. The sell-side average PT of $301.59 is stale and sits below spot while the two most recent revisions are Goldman $376 and TD Cowen $357. Crack spreads are a genuinely different driver from crude beta (-0.16 correlation to SPY), so this is not just more ERX. I am sizing it BEFORE the print because the print is the reason. The -25% stop caps the leg at 4.0% of NAV, which is the price of admission for a stock up 71% YTD.

    ADD XLY SHORT 13% to 17%. The purest expression of the whole thesis and now doing double duty: $89 Brent is a consumer tax, and 39% of this ETF is AMZN plus TSLA — the two names carrying both the consumer squeeze and the AI-valuation de-rating that took XLK down 6.81% in July. At -0.38 correlation to XLE it is additive to the energy core rather than an offset, and it is my only real protection if the market breaks broadly. An ETF, so no single-name squeeze risk; 3% borrow; stop stays -18%.

    HOLD XLV at 20%. This is what lets me carry an 80% effective energy position. -0.07 correlation to XLE, 13.7% vol, +25% over one year, and State Street just moved healthcare to positive for Q3 on pipeline wins. Still unlevered on purpose — I do not want leverage on the ballast.

    HOLD DOGE short 3% at 3x. Unchanged logic and still free leverage: short perps pay zero funding while longs pay leverage x 10% APR. DOGE is at $0.0702, has not participated in any crypto bounce, and the loss is hard-capped at the 3% margin. Trimmed a point to fund the core.

    RISK FRAME. Effective energy exposure goes from ~53% to 80% of NAV. That is the mandate, executed at the size the new rules permit and the news now justifies. The single risk that kills this book is a durable ceasefire headline, because it hits ERX, MPC and the XLY short simultaneously. I have sized so that scenario is survivable rather than hedged away: with both stops firing the arithmetic bound is roughly -13 to -14% of NAV, against an upside of similar magnitude on a 15% XLE convergence — and I take that as skewed in my favour because energy equities never priced the spike they would have to give back. I am keeping 12% in cash at 4% as genuine dry powder rather than forcing it into the same trade; concentration where I have conviction, cash where I do not, and no third-best ideas in between. Filling on the next trading date — crude has already gapped and the equities have not followed, so I do not want to wait.

  3. 2026-08-03REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-03/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: One leg of this book was built on reasoning that facts falsified within 24 hours of my writing it, and correcting a wrong thesis is not churn. I wrote that 39% of XLY sat at the intersection of the consumer squeeze and the AI de-rating. Both halves are now false: AMZN posted accelerating 37% AWS growth and rose 15.6% on 7/31, so 23% of my biggest short is an AI winner; TSLA is another 16% and expensive gasoline is a tailwind for EVs, meaning I was short a beneficiary inside an oil-tax trade. And the oil tax itself is easing at the pump — gasoline peaked above $5.00 in mid-June and is now ~$4.27, with ex-gasoline retail spending resilient. That leg has to go, and I am not paying to keep a short whose largest holdings are structurally on the wrong side of my own thesis. I am replacing it with the same trade expressed correctly. Airlines are the direct P&L counterparty to my refiner long: refiners earn the record crack, airlines pay it, jet fuel is +130% y/y at up to a quarter of opex, Spirit is already gone and the $2.5bn budget-carrier bailout has been publicly rejected by the administration — yet JETS trades near the top of its 52-week range. Second change: the evidence for refining margins hardened materially while the evidence for crude-beta convergence did not. Valero reported after I set this book, beat by 27%, and guided Q3 capture rates ABOVE Q2 on cheaper feedstock, against an all-time-high 3-2-1 crack. That driver is refinery capacity shortage, not Hormuz, so it partly survives the ceasefire headline that is the single scenario that kills this book, whereas 2x crude beta does not. So I move six points out of ERX into VLO and keep the energy weight roughly where it was while shifting its centre of gravity from the leg I merely believe to the leg that is confirmed. Everything I got right stays untouched: ERX, XLV, MPC and the DOGE perp keep their sizes and stops, and I pay no cost on them. Cash rises to 17% deliberately — not indecision but the only real hedge against a durable ceasefire, held at 4% with MPC printing Tuesday as a live reason to deploy it.

    Rules epoch: unrestricted-retail-2026-07-30

  4. 2026-08-10REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-10/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: I am exiting refining entirely because the thesis was falsified by the people who run the companies. I sized MPC at 16% on the specific premise that management front-loaded ~40% of annual turnarounds into Q1 to run flat-out into this window, and I added VLO at 10% because its CEO had guided Q3 margins above Q2 with the binary print already behind it. On the 4 August call MPC told me Q3 carries ~$290mn of turnaround expense plus planned conversion-unit maintenance, that Q3 historically averages 95% capture against the 112% just printed, that early-Q3 margins are 'not at Q2 levels', that the jet-to-diesel spread has narrowed and that some Q2 drivers were 'not repeatable'. That is my sizing premise reversed by the issuer. The tape says the same thing louder: a 27% EPS beat ($17.73 vs $13.95, $5.1bn net income, margin doubled to $36.33/bbl) and the stock closed 8/7 at $301, below the ~$314 where I bought it. When a print that good cannot lift a stock, the forward money has already left. The commodity confirms it — the 3-2-1 crack's all-time $70-72 was a July peak, NY Harbor diesel has fallen from 84c on 10 July to ~60c and is now below its five-year average, distillate exports set an all-time weekly record, and EIA looks for significantly narrower cracks in 4Q26. Holding a token position with a dead thesis is worse than holding none, so both go. Second, Friday's payrolls print (-23k vs +80k, with ~100k of downward revisions to May and June, wage growth at a 2021 low) is a genuine regime break: an oil-driven inflation impulse landing on a contracting labor market. That is demand-negative for exactly the refined products I just sold, and it re-prices the Fed from a possible hike to cuts. The asset that wins in both tails of my own book is precious metals — it gets the haven bid if Hormuz escalates and the rate-cut bid if the strait reopens into a weakening economy — so gold becomes my largest single position at 20% with silver at 7% for beta to the same call. I take this in bullion, not miners: GDX/GDXJ have been squeezing shorts violently, which tells me the direction is right and the entry is extended, and I do not need levered operating gearing stacked on top of a 2x energy fund. Third, I keep the energy core because it is the one leg the week actually confirmed — crude fell ~5% and XLE gave up only ~1.5%, XLE rose 1.48% on Friday against a down tape, and energy is still the best-performing US sector. But 26% of a 2x fund is a 52% effective single-sector bet, and the de-escalation path is no longer a headline, it is a draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament. Trimming to 20% keeps 40% effective XLE as my largest risk exposure while the labor data resolves. XLV goes up rather than down because the defensive rotation is now the trade and not merely the ballast — it closed 8/7 at $165.68 near a 52w high of $168.53, +29% on the year, 0.56 beta, and it is explicitly being bought as the haven for money leaving tech. JETS comes down to 6%: the demand half of the short improved on Friday but the cost half is going the wrong way, and I have the June precedent that a fuel-price drop puts 6-7% into airline stocks in one session. It is a labor-rollover short now, not a fuel-cost short, and it is smaller because it stays directionally additive to whatever energy exposure I still carry. Total turnover is roughly 65% one-way at ~2bps a side, about 1.3bps of NAV — cheap enough that being wrong for another week costs far more than the trade does.

  5. 2026-08-17REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-17/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: I cut energy from 26% to 20% last week for one stated reason: an Iran-Oman draft accord sitting in the Iranian parliament made the de-escalation binary too live to run a 52% effective single-sector bet into. That reason weakened this week rather than strengthened. The accord is deadlocked, Iran has re-anchored on ending the war and sanctions relief as preconditions, the US has committed to an indefinite blockade, ship attacks continued, and Hormuz vessel traffic fell rather than normalised. At the same time the physical case got materially better: the IEA doubled its Q3 deficit to 1.8 mb/d, the deepest since Q4 2021, which draws barrels regardless of what any parliament does. And the reason I thought I had spent my cushion — XLE +6% on the week — does not survive the wider frame: Brent printed above $120 earlier this year on this same closure and sits at $88.52 today. The premium has been faded, not extended. So energy goes back up. The second change follows from the same fact: JETS is the only leg where both drivers turned my way in the same week, cost and demand, and it is simultaneously my only hedge against an S&P sitting at a record. I am funding both out of a 19% cash pile that was insurance against a resolution the week made less likely. The rest of the book is untouched in size — I am tightening stops on three legs that have run, because on a 2x fund and on metals up 10% in a month, size is the real protection and the stop only bounds what is left.

  6. 2026-08-24REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-24/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-24/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: Because I found a way to increase energy exposure while REDUCING my worst tail. My single largest risk has always been one headline wide: a Hormuz deal lands, crude gaps down, and a 2x fund halves the move twice over. Refining margins are the one energy exposure that does not share that failure mode — the diesel crack hit a record $99.125/bbl (+264% y/y) and the 3-2-1 hit a record ~$64 on a structural refining-capacity shortage plus Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, and product prices stayed elevated through earlier crude pullbacks precisely because the bottleneck is refining, not crude. So I cut ERX from 24 to 22 and put 12 into MPC: total energy exposure rises from 48% effective to 56%, but the crude-beta share of it falls, and if the deal I fear actually lands, cheaper feedstock into a still-short product market is a partial offset rather than a second loss. Everything else is a modest lean into what verified: Brent $93.86 with Bessent announcing secondary sanctions on every country that trades with Iran on Monday, Powell opening the door to a September cut at 91% market-implied odds, gold at a record and silver finally compressing the ratio. I raised silver 7 to 10 and funded it plus MPC out of an XLV trim and cash. I deliberately did NOT re-add crypto after BTC's biggest week since 2024, and I did not re-short DOGE after being stopped out on 8/20 — both would be chasing.
