  7. 2026-08-31REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-31/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-31/opus5_unrestricted.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two of my three stated premises broke this week and I am not going to hold positions whose written reasons are now false. The ERX thesis was supply removal — blockade plus 'toughest sanctions in history.' The sanctions landed softer than billed, Iran and Oman announced a phased Hormuz corridor framework with joint mine-clearing, Gulf exports have recovered from 5-6 mb/d in March to 15-16 mb/d, and Brent fell 5%+ to ~$88.5. That is my named worst tail arriving in slow motion rather than as a gap, which is the version where I actually get to act on it. The GLD and SLV sizes were justified in writing by '91% odds of a September cut'; Warsh used his first Jackson Hole speech to put rate HIKES in play, the two-year moved to 4.30%, and September hike odds are near 50%. Meanwhile the one leg that does not depend on either premise got materially stronger: the diesel crack printed a record $102.20, sits near $93-94, distillate inventories are at a 30-year low, 7-8 mb/d of refining capacity is offline, and MPC made an all-time high in the same week crude fell 5%. Cheaper crude is a feedstock tailwind to the crack, not a headwind. So I am selling the barrel and buying the bottleneck: ERX 22 to 8, MPC 12 to 20, new VLO 10, and the book's center of gravity moves from 'crude goes up' to 'refined products stay scarce' — a thesis that survives the de-escalation that is killing the old one and is paired against a short in the product's captive consumer. Metals go 30 to 19 because their engine reversed, not to zero, because gold held $4,608 through an explicitly hawkish Jackson Hole on record central-bank buying. Cash to 13 because a Fed that may hike makes 4%+ a real competing asset, and because I just cut my highest-conviction directional bet and do not want to force the proceeds somewhere to avoid looking idle.

  8. 2026-09-08REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-08/opus5_unrestricted.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-08/opus5_unrestricted.json

    My own tape settled three arguments this week and I am acting on all three. (1) The crack, not crude, is the trade. Crude had its best week since 13 July (WTI +8.8% to ~$92, Brent ~$95-97 on Iranian strikes into Kuwait and Hormuz shipping disruption), yet my 2x levered energy leg ERX returned +0.32% while MPC returned +4.17% and VLO +3.29%. A 2x crude-beta ETF that cannot make money on a +8.8% crude week is telling me the market refuses to capitalise E&P earnings from a war premium it expects to reverse. ERX also costs 5bps a side plus daily-rebalance decay. It goes to zero weight. (2) Gold is trading on the rate channel, not the war channel. In a week where Iran struck a Gulf state and diesel cracks set an all-time record, GLD fell 0.40% and SLV fell 0.52%, then gold dropped another 1.3% Friday to ~$4,420 when August payrolls printed 162k against a ~55k consensus and revived September hike bets (Kalshi/market odds swinging in the 50-64% range on a 3.50-3.75% funds rate). I have no edge in a metal whose dominant driver over my holding window is a CPI print on ~11 Sep and an FOMC on 16 Sep that both skew hawkish. Both metals legs go to zero and the capital sits in cash at 4%. (3) My short JETS failed in the single most favourable week it will ever get. Crude +8.8%, jet crack at records, and airlines still rose ~1.05% against me. That is a fully priced, one-sided short. I am not just closing it, I am reversing it small: a 6% long in JETS is the only cheap instrument that pays if the crack normalises, which is exactly the scenario that hurts a 62% refiner book. Refiners are long the crack; airlines are short it. The residual is my actual view, held deliberately and at a size I chose. What I am buying instead is more of the one thing that demonstrably worked, spread across four operators so a single refinery fire or turnaround cannot break the thesis. The US diesel crack broke $106/bbl on 1 September, an all-time record, and the WTI 3-2-1 crack sits near $59 versus roughly a third of that in January. The cause is physical and slow to repair: Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian refineries plus a Russian fuel export ban, damaged Middle East refineries, and Hormuz disruption that Mitsui O.S.K. expects to persist into next year. Refining capacity is not rebuilt in a quarter. The valuation is my margin of safety: VLO at 8.7x forward earnings after $3.7bn of Q2 net income, DINO at 10.1x with adjusted refinery margin up 57% y/y to $25.95/bbl, PBF at 6.4x on $11.56 TTM EPS. Sell-side price targets sit BELOW market on all of them, which means consensus has not marked to the current margin environment and Q3 prints in late October will be reported against stale numbers. The risk I am accepting and naming: this is one factor, refiners are up 80-175% in 2026, CNBC flagged the run as near-unprecedented and due to mean-revert, and Vice President Vance has publicly said Iran's ability to control Hormuz is 'effectively gone', which is the ceasefire tell. A comprehensive de-escalation next week is roughly a 8-10% hit to this book after the JETS and XLV offsets. I have sized for that: gross exposure falls from 87% to 82%, cash rises from 13% to 18% ahead of two macro events, and every cyclical leg carries a hard stop.

Management at the weekly reassessment is explicitly regime-driven and mechanical: if SPY 20d realized vol rises through roughly 18% or the 10d/60d ratio moves above 1.3, I cut SVXY toward zero, cut the short-gamma pair (trend is its enemy), raise VIXY and cash, and rotate the equity core further toward USMV; if realized vol falls back under 10% with VIX still near 18 I add to SVXY and the decay pair. If dispersion compresses — the implied-correlation proxy climbing back toward 0.55 — the case for holding low-vol equity over the index weakens and I would move the core toward broader beta. The specific thing that would make me abandon the construction is realized vol printing above implied for several weeks, which would mean the premium I am being paid has gone negative.

THE CENTRAL CAVEAT: a static allocation cannot switch regimes mid-window, which is the entire point of the strategy. These three windows therefore test whether the CURRENT regime call (calm index, high dispersion, wide variance premium) would have survived three different historical tapes — they do NOT test the switching rule, which only becomes visible across weekly reassessments in the live round. The book underperforms SPY by 4.6 and 8.2 points in the two rising windows and beats it by 8.5 points in the stress window; that asymmetry is the intended character, not a defect, but it means a sustained melt-up is the most likely way this book finishes behind. STOP DESIGN, FOUND BY ITERATION: an earlier candidate carried 30% stops on both leveraged-ETF legs and returned -5.92% with a -11.20% drawdown in 2026H1, because a whipsaw stopped out first one leg and then the other, twice converting a hedged pair into a naked directional short; removing the per-leg stops took the same window to +1.62% and the stress window from -0.05% to +7.83%. The pair is therefore risk-controlled by SIZE and by the natural floor on a short, not by stops. SVXY's stop was likewise widened from 18% to 25% after the tighter level fired at the March-2026 vol bump and locked in a loss the position then recovered. SHORT-VOL TAIL RISK, STATED PLAINLY: the accepted loss on a 1-day -21% / 5-day -34% SVXY event is about -3 to -4% of NAV after the stop, partly offset by VIXY, and the engine only checks stops at daily closes, so an intraday gap would fill worse than the stop level. In the stress window SVXY hit its stop and VIXY hit its take-profit (the engine prints these closures as LIQUIDATED) and the book still finished +5.47%, which is the hedge working as designed. Other caveats: no market impact or borrow-availability constraint on the leveraged-ETF shorts, flat 3% borrow and 10% funding, and daily-close granularity throughout.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-01: I am not touching the equity core, which is a session old and needs no change; I am closing the two carry legs because one had its premise refuted overnight and the other was already refuted by my own arithmetic. SVXY existed to harvest the gap between implied and realized index vol. When I sized it that gap was ~7 points; after VIX collapsed 22% to ~16 against SPY realized of ~13-14% it is ~2-3 points. Getting paid 2-3 points to be short the tail is thin at the best of times, and this is not the best of times: the 10y just broke to 4.75% on $100 oil and an escalating Middle East conflict, which is precisely the macro shock that drags implied correlation back up and hurts a short-index-vol position most. The carry shrank and the tail fattened simultaneously, so the leg goes. The TQQQ/SQQQ pair is me correcting a documented mistake rather than reacting to news: on 7/30 I wrote that my own backtest gives it ~1.2%/yr on notional against 3% APR borrow on EACH leg — roughly -0.25% of NAV per year with a -27.76% worst 63-day — and then kept it at 7+7 anyway because it 'expressed the regime.' That was attachment to a narrative over my own numbers. It is a negative-carry structure whose best environment is chop and whose worst is trend, and an oil-and-rates shock is a trending catalyst, so the case only got weaker. Closing both costs about 26% turnover at ~2-2.5bps, roughly $0.07, and it is economically positive from day one: I stop paying 0.42%/yr of NAV in borrow and start earning 4% on the cash. VIXY goes up rather than down as the exact mirror of my 7/30 trim — I cut it then because buying insurance at VIX 20.66 right after a pop is paying up post-event, and the same insurance now costs ~22% less in VIX terms while the event it insures against became materially more likely. Buy convexity when it is cheap and the tail is fat; that is the discipline, and it is the reason I can still run an 78% low-vol equity core. The 16% cash is deliberate, not a residual: with my short-vol carry removed and a live geopolitical/inflation catalyst, dry powder that pays 4% is the right way to hold risk in reserve, and it funds adding to the core if the rate shock hands me a better entry. Net result is a simpler book, lower gross, no borrow, more cash yield, and my two best-evidenced legs plus a cheap hedge.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-08: Two things moved enough to force this, and they point the same way. First, the volatility risk premium has closed: VIX 15.15 against SPY 20d realized 13.49% is ~1.7 points, versus a ~3-4 point norm, so index vol is no longer expensive - and Cboe implied correlation sits at a 23-year low (COR3M ~9-10, 52-week range 9.29-11.95), which is a bounded, mean-reverting quantity that can only normalise upward. Long index vol therefore pays if realized rises OR correlation normalises, and the compressed contango (VX6/VX1 1.062 vs a 1.15-1.20 norm) means I pay a third-to-half the carry I underwrote at entry. Cheaper insurance against a denser calendar - CPI 12-Aug, a stalled Hormuz fee dispute with Brent at $80, and a 15-16 Sep FOMC where a Warsh hike is still 44% priced after payrolls printed -23k with 103k of downward revisions. Second, and this is the correction I owe myself: I have been conflating vol targeting with owning low-vol stocks. Vol targeting scales exposure to the INDEX by the index's realized vol. USMV and SPLV buy their low vol by surrendering expected return and by parking 25% of SPLV in utilities ahead of a live hike; the index buys its low vol from diversification, which is free and is at a 23-year maximum precisely because correlation is at a 23-year low. At COR3M ~10 the S&P realizes 13.5% while its average constituent realizes far more - that makes SPY the cheapest carrier of equity risk in my universe right now, not USMV. My book was carrying only ~40 SPY-equivalent betas into a low-correlation, low-index-vol tape and made +0.97% while the index made +3.58% and tech made +7.2%. The fix is not to abandon defence, it is to take the permission the insurance already bought: raise index beta and raise the hedge together. Modelled across three states - calm melt-up, moderate scare, and a VIX-doubling shock - the new shape beats the old one in every one, because more cheap convexity is what makes more beta affordable rather than a substitute for it.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-15: Two pieces of my own evidence turned against last week's construction and one turned against last week's arithmetic, so this is a correction rather than a view change - the regime call (calm index, violent components) is unchanged and this book expresses it better.

    First, the arithmetic. I built a 40% SPY core on 'index variance equals average constituent variance times correlation', arguing the cap-weighted wrapper is safer than its contents at a 23-year correlation low. That identity is an equal-weight identity. RSP realizes 9.79% at 20d and 10.92% at 60d against SPY's 13.33% and 13.93%, on the same tape in the same window - the equal-weighted index captures the diversification benefit I was describing while SPY's megacap concentration consumes most of it. I checked this was not a 20-day artefact before acting on it: over the trailing year RSP returned +21.8% against SPY's +22.0% with a smaller max drawdown (-7.9% vs -8.9%) and roughly 68% average downside capture across SPY's eight worst days. Identical return, a quarter less volatility, at all three horizons. If my mandate is return per unit of realized vol, RSP is simply the better vehicle for the exact thesis I already hold, so 30% moves to RSP and SPY keeps 20% because I am correcting an expression, not abandoning cap-weighted beta entirely.

    Second, the carry. VIXM/VIXY moved +3.9% in five sessions against a ~1.1%/week three-month average; netting each ETF's beta to spot leaves roughly a point a week of excess front-month decay, about 50% annualised. On 08-08 I explicitly justified upsizing VIXY to 11% on the claim that compressed contango had cut my roll cost to a third-to-a-half of the 43.8%/yr underwritten at entry. That claim is now false by my own measurement. Separately, the value case has thinned: VIX 14.25 against 10d realized 11.64% is 2.6 points of premium, near normal, and realized is falling faster than implied. I am not abandoning the hedge - VVIX at 87 is cheap convexity, SKEW rose to 138 in a week VIX fell, and the 15-16 Sep FOMC is a dated live binary inside my horizon - but a leg whose price of carry has doubled while its value case thinned should shrink to true insurance size, so 11% goes to 7% with the take-profit untouched.

    Third, SPLV. I kept it for tech-free diversification, but its protection is a rates bet and rates went the wrong way: ^TNX to 4.70 with ^IRX pinned at 3.70, a long-end-led steepening, which is precisely the inflation-expectations move an +7.9% Brent week produces. XLU -2.55% and SPLV -0.57% on the month confirm it. Once RSP is in the book, SPLV's broad-diversification role is redundant and only its concentrated utilities bet remains, so I exit it.

    What replaces it is the reason I am comfortable cutting the vol sleeve. XLE printed positive on five of SPY's eight worst days of the trailing year - better crash behaviour than SPLV's four of eight - while returning +49.2% over that year against SPLV's +6.2%. It is long the one macro shock actually running (Brent +7.9%, XLE +7.7%, USO +7.3% in a week the S&P gained 0.4% and VIX fell), and an energy-led inflation impulse is the single state where SPY, USMV and cash all lose together and only my hedges help. Sized at just 7% because it realizes 24.5% vol and because a leg that ran 7.7% in five sessions deserves respect, not enthusiasm. The net effect is a book with the same equity beta, materially less realized volatility, a hedge that earns rather than bleeds, and 18% cash at 4% into a live September Fed.

    Weekly desk 2026-08-22: The regime call was right and paid - the book made +0.30% while SPY lost 1.37% - so this is not a view change. It is a correction of where the hedge sits. I built this book to be hedged against an energy-inflation shock and then measured, for the first time, what each leg actually does when that shock arrives: regressed on daily 30y yield changes and ranked against the twelve largest yield-up days of the year, XLE is the ONLY long leg I own with positive rate beta (+1.86%/10bp at 60d, 8/12 positive, avg +0.72%), while SPY is -0.57, RSP -0.91 and USMV -0.40. The risk I named is now the one actually running - the 30y printed 5.31% this week, a 19-year high, on fiscal supply and term premium rather than policy - and I was carrying 7% against it and 68% exposed to it. Two dated catalysts sit inside the horizon and both push the same way: Bessent's Iran measures Monday 08-24 with Brent already +13% over two weeks on persistent Hormuz shut-ins, and Warsh's debut Jackson Hole keynote Friday 08-28, where September is now priced ~1-in-3 for a HIKE with three standing dissents already voted for one. So I double the macro hedge to 15% and fund it by trimming SPY from 20% to 14%, which is the same trade twice: a term-premium shock is a discount-rate shock and it hits the longest-duration cash flows hardest, which is precisely SPY's ~40% megacap concentration - XLK -3.53%, SMH -4.66%, Meta -7% in a week SPY lost 1.37% and RSP lost 0.49%. That is a mechanism, not the leadership forecast I said last week I did not have. I split the hedge across XLE and COMT rather than loading XLE alone because ~15% of XLE is refiners whose crack spreads can compress on exactly the transit-disruption shock I am hedging, and because XOM+CVX are 35% of the fund. Backtested over the trailing year the new book returns +14.02% against the current book's +11.83% at 5.03% vol vs 4.86% and -2.34% max drawdown vs -2.11%, with a better ten-worst-day average (-0.25% vs -0.37%) - more return, better crash behaviour, marginally more vol, and every variant I tested beat the incumbent, so the improvement is robust to the exact weights rather than fitted to them. VIXY stays at 7% despite finding the cheapest VIX convexity in two years (VVIX 2nd percentile, VIX minus rv20 at the 27th percentile against a 4.11 mean): I ran the sizing test before acting and across a year containing ten sessions worse than -1.5%, every extra point of VIXY above 7% cost more carry than it returned. Turnover is ~14% of NAV at 2bp a side, under a basis point all in.

  7. 2026-08-31REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-31/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-08-31/opus5_volregime.json

    Weekly desk 2026-08-29: Two facts moved in opposite directions and the correct response is to move risk between hedges rather than to add or shed any. First, the driver behind my commodity hedge reversed: Brent peaked at 94.39 on 08-21 and closed 89.70, -4.97% off the high, and I raised XLE from 7% to 9% exactly seven days ago citing that rally by name. Sizing to a driver means cutting when the driver decays, so XLE goes to 6%. Second, the event my volatility hedge exists for became substantially more likely while its price fell to a sample floor: the desk reports Warsh's hawkish Jackson Hole repriced the 09-16 FOMC from 34% to 57% odds of a HIKE - twelve trading days inside my horizon, and a direction no equity leg I own is positioned for - while VVIX printed 82.90, the 0th percentile of my two-year sample. So VIXY goes from 7% to 9%. I am adding to the leg that lost the most since entry (-4.88%), and the reason is that it got cheaper while what it insures got more probable, which is the only good reason to add to a loser. I am deliberately honest that my headline argument for owning vol last week has weakened: VIX minus rv20 went from 1.98 points at the 27th percentile to 3.97 at the 41st, which is exactly average - the vol level is no longer cheap, only its convexity is, and that is why this is a two-point add rather than the five my enthusiasm wanted. My own backtest still says every marginal point of VIXY costs about a point of annual return. What makes the swap defensible rather than a hunch is that it improves the book on the measures I care about while leaving rate protection untouched: trailing-year volatility 5.00 -> 4.75, max drawdown -2.29 -> -2.27, ten-worst-day average -0.25 -> -0.10, twelve-yield-up-day average -0.07 -> -0.08. Everything else holds. I am not touching RSP after one week in which it lagged SPY by 58bp, because I wrote last week that I refuse to trade on a single window, and a week where megacap tech leads is precisely the state the equal-weight tilt is supposed to lag. Total turnover is 5% of gross, about a basis point of cost.

  8. 2026-09-08REBALANCERegistered rebalance · experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-08/opus5_volregime.json
    Registered book note — experiments/round3/weeks/2026-09-08/opus5_volregime.json

    Last week I classified the tape as calm-index / high-dispersion and sized to harvest the variance risk premium (SVXY short vol, 60% vol-targeted low-vol equity, a short-gamma leveraged-ETF pair). Three things changed and they invert that call. (1) Implied vol has fallen to a floor, not to a fair level: VIX closed 14.53 on 2026-09-04, the 6.2nd percentile of two years, and VVIX closed 84.42, the 1.2nd percentile and within 3 points of its two-year low of 81.89 - convexity on volatility itself has literally never been cheaper in my sample. Selling vol at the 6th percentile pays a few points of carry for unbounded left-tail; the VRP has compressed from the ~7 points I sized to (VIX 18.6 vs RV 11.65) to ~6.4 points at half the absolute level, so the same dollar of short-vol risk now earns far less. (2) The macro risk that vol is supposed to price has gone to a two-year HIGH at exactly the same time. August payrolls printed 162k against a 55k consensus with unemployment steady at 4.1%; PCE is running 3.7%; the 5y (4.55%) and 10y (4.78%) closed at the 98.8th and 99.0th percentile of two years, effectively at their two-year highs; and fed funds futures now price roughly 50-58% odds of a rate HIKE at the September 15-16 FOMC, which also carries a Summary of Economic Projections. CPI and PPI land before it. That means three live macro catalysts fall inside six or seven sessions of my 2026-09-08 entry, and the equity vol surface is pricing them as a non-event. Note also that SKEW has climbed from 143 to 151.6 over two weeks while ATM vol fell - someone is paying up for tails while the ATM strip melts, which is the signature of a market that is complacent at the money and nervous in the wings. (3) My own book is on the wrong side of the rate regime. RSP plus USMV was 48% of NAV in equal-weight and minimum-volatility equity, both of which carry heavy bond-proxy and duration sensitivity; with the long end at two-year highs and a hiking Fed live, that is a short-rates-vol position dressed as a defensive one, and it shows in the tape - SPLV is -1.81% over a month and -0.64% over six, USMV +5.05% over six against SPY +15.16%, and the book is -0.25% for the round against SPY +3.62%. So I am replacing rather than holding. The regime call is that index volatility is mispriced low relative to identifiable event risk, while sector-level volatility is being realized at the 60th-80th percentile (XLE 21.3, COMT 18.7, GLD 27.1, GDX 51.2, XLV 18.9) - a very low implied-correlation state. The correct expression is to own the convexity while it is cheap, to take equity risk only where volatility is actually being paid, to hold nothing whose main risk is duration, and to let cash at 4% carry the rest rather than manufacture carry by selling a 6th-percentile vol surface. Turnover is roughly half the book; at 2bps a side that costs a few basis points, which is trivial against the risk of being short gamma into a coin-flip hike.

Added GDX long (13%): gold miners have broken through prior highs even as gold itself hasn't cleared its equivalent resistance (miners leading the metal, a classic leveraged-reversion setup), and GDX's free-cash-flow/EV yield is at record highs with forward multiples at five-year lows -- a legitimate mean-reversion-to-fair-value trade the book never held despite the mandate naming it explicitly (note: this book's one prior GDX attempt was stopped out, so sized modestly). That is a real regime signal, not noise -- it flipped the market narrative from expecting Fed cuts to pricing meaningfully higher odds of the Fed staying hawkish (or even hiking), which lifted the dollar and Treasury yields and knocked gold down on the day even as Trump publicly pressured the Fed to cut. That directly cuts against this book's 'dollar-debasement hedge' rationale for GLD in the near term, so I'm trimming it rather than either exiting outright or ignoring the data -- the structural bull case (Goldman $4,900 and RBC ~$5,000 year-end targets, continued central-bank buying/repatriation such as the Netherlands moving ~86t of gold out of New York, and persistent debt-debasement flows) is still intact and unrefuted by one data print, so a reduced core position is the right sizing rather than zero. On the other side of the book, FXI actually traded up this week (+1.5% on the day) into a real near-term catalyst: the U.S. and China are reportedly finalizing agriculture and non-tariff-barrier announcements around Xi's upcoming Washington visit, and China's July exports beat expectations on AI-linked high-tech demand -- so I'm adding modestly there rather than to the now-more-crowded, more-uncertain rate-cut trade. I'm not adding new industrial/capex-reacceleration or small-cap exposure this week: IWM sentiment pieces (Wells Fargo, Goldman) flag deteriorating small-cap earnings revisions under the rally, and semis/AI-capex commentary is split between 'buy the dip' (JPMorgan) and 'another 10% down, hard remainder of 2026' (Morgan Stanley) plus a fresh tariff threat on chip/server/laptop imports -- too two-sided to fund a new leg out of cash. Net effect: keep the book intentionally light (10% gross, 90% cash earning 4%) and let this week's real macro surprise, not habit, drive the one adjustment worth making.

    This book's core premise -- imminent Fed rate cuts driving a carry trade in regional banks, financials and small caps -- was directly contradicted by this week's data. The August jobs report (released Sept 4-5) beat estimates hard enough that Fed funds futures for the Sept 16 FOMC swung from a plurality favoring a cut to now pricing better-than-even odds (~58%) of a HIKE to 3.75-4.00%, an 8-point swing in a single day. KRE and IWM were already leaking lower into the print (KRE -1.00%, IWM -1.32% on this book's marks) and broader coverage this week was explicitly framing strong jobs data as bad news for risk assets ('stocks close lower... stir rate-hike jitters'). There is no case for holding a rate-cut-carry book into a meeting the market now thinks is more likely to hike than cut, so I am exiting KRE and XLF outright and closing the IWM long rather than let the same repricing that already knocked ~1-1.3% off them keep compounding. I am keeping XBI, but re-underwriting it as a standalone biotech M&A idea rather than a rate-cut play -- Eli Lilly's newly announced acquisition this week is fresh evidence the large-pharma consolidation cycle is alive independent of Fed policy, and XBI is still +3.66% on this book's own entry. In place of the exited carry longs I am adding the mandate's other pillar -- momentum-breakdown shorts in gold miners and crypto majors -- with actual evidence behind it this week rather than waiting: Bitcoin broke back below $80k specifically on the rate-hike repricing, with BTC ETF net inflows collapsing 76% in a single day, and gold/gold-miner equities carry direct negative sensitivity to rising real-rate expectations (GDX short already fired once via this book's standing order this cycle, so the setup has precedent). Raising cash to 61% (from 36%) reflects that the FOMC outcome is now a genuine coin-flip rather than a settled cutting cycle, and this is not the week to be levered into that uncertainty.

Key findings: (1) Bitcoin at $63-64k represents ~50% bear drawdown from $126k peak - capitulation thesis validating but reversal uncertain given ETF outflows and Fed holding rates; (2) Tech/AI shows exhaustion signals (QQQ -10% from peak, technical breakdown, MACD crossover) despite strong TSMC/NVIDIA earnings, with Aug 1 tariff deadline adding headwind; (3) China rotation thesis falsified - EM ex-China up 38% YTD while China drags; capital rotating OUT not IN; (4) Japan performing well (EWJ +15-36% YTD, hitting all-time highs) but recent 2-day Nikkei pullback; (5) Value/dividend rotation accelerating (flows $1.96B into financials, $1.47B into healthcare; XLF/XLE/XLV all strong); (6) Financial sector dividend yields at 5.69% average with subsectors higher (9%+). Round 3 strategy validating perfectly (+0.91% with -0.42% max drawdown). Round 2 down 4.42% with broken theses (China rotation, tech leverage drag).

Recorded once per manager in experiments/desk/unrestricted_resize_2026-07-30.json and copied verbatim into that manager’s 2026-07-31 books.

The desk refuses to re-weight a book on a guess, so (a) stands and this book is flagged for the manager to restate its intent at the next poll.

Federal Reserve held rates at 3.50%-3.75% on July 28-29 with three dissents preferring a hike; 10Y Treasury yield rose 7bp to 4.67%. S&P 500 declined 1.52% despite MSFT beat, reflecting market concerns about semiconductor valuations and Fed hawkishness. Semiconductor sector under pressure (Nasdaq 100 down 11% from highs), but Russell 2000 continues strong performance (+20% YTD, best year since 2003). Energy sector strong (+34% YTD) on geopolitical and AI infrastructure demand. Financial sector continues to benefit from yield curve steepening (10Y-2Y at +52bp). Salesforce (CRM) remains oversold with recovery drivers intact (Agentforce $1.4B revenue +114% YoY, $25B buyback). Cryptocurrency stabilizing with Bitcoin at $64K and Ethereum at $1,920, down significantly YTD but showing relative stabilization after Fed meeting.
